# capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/

## Expand description

An implementation of the [Cap’n Proto remote procedure call](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html)
protocol. Includes all [Level 1](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#protocol-features) features.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
# Cap'n Proto schema
interface Foo {
    identity @0 (x: UInt32) -> (y: UInt32);
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Rust server defining an implementation of Foo.
struct FooImpl;
impl foo::Server for FooImpl {
    async fn identity(
        self: Rc<Self>,
        params: foo::IdentityParams,
        mut results: foo::IdentityResults
    ) -> Result<(), ::capnp::Error> {
        let x = params.get()?.get_x();
        results.get().set_y(x);
        Ok(())
    }
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Rust client calling a remote implementation of Foo.
let mut request = foo_client.identity_request();
request.get().set_x(123);
let promise = request.send().promise.and_then(|response| {
    println!("results = {}", response.get()?.get_y());
    Ok(())
});
```
For a more complete example, see [https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [rpc_](https://docs.rs/rpc_capnp/index.html)- capnp
- Code generated from
[rpc.capnp](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/master/c%2B%2B/src/capnp/rpc.capnp).
- [rpc_](https://docs.rs/rpc_twoparty_capnp/index.html)- twoparty_ - capnp
- Code generated from
[rpc-twoparty.capnp](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/master/c%2B%2B/src/capnp/rpc-twoparty.capnp).
- [twoparty](https://docs.rs/twoparty/index.html)
- An implementation of `VatNetwork`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [pry](https://docs.rs/macro.pry.html)
- Like `try!()``Promise<T, E>``Result<T, E>`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Capability](https://docs.rs/struct.CapabilityServerSet.html)- Server - Set
- Collection of unwrappable capabilities.
- [Disconnector](https://docs.rs/struct.Disconnector.html)
- A `Future`that can be run to disconnect an`RpcSystem`’s ConnectionState and wait for it to be closed.
- [Imbued](https://docs.rs/struct.ImbuedMessageBuilder.html)- Message - Builder
- [RpcSystem](https://docs.rs/struct.RpcSystem.html)
- A portal to objects available on the network.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Connection](https://docs.rs/trait.Connection.html)
- A two-way RPC connection.
- [Flow](https://docs.rs/trait.FlowController.html)- Controller
- Tracks a particular RPC stream in order to implement a flow control algorithm.
- [Incoming](https://docs.rs/trait.IncomingMessage.html)- Message
- A message received from a `VatNetwork`
- [Outgoing](https://docs.rs/trait.OutgoingMessage.html)- Message
- A message to be sent by a `VatNetwork`
- [SetTarget](https://docs.rs/trait.SetTarget.html)
- Trait implemented by the reconnecting client to set new connection out-of-band.
- [VatNetwork](https://docs.rs/trait.VatNetwork.html)
- Network facility between vats, it determines how to form connections between vats.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [auto_](https://docs.rs/fn.auto_reconnect.html)- reconnect
- Creates a new client that reconnects when getting `ErrorKind::Disconnected`
- [lazy_](https://docs.rs/fn.lazy_auto_reconnect.html)- auto_ - reconnect
- Creates a new client that lazily connect and also reconnects when getting `ErrorKind::Disconnected`
- [new_](https://docs.rs/fn.new_client.html)- client
- Creates a new local RPC client of type `C`out of an object that implements a server trait`S`.
- [new_](https://docs.rs/fn.new_client_from_rc.html)- client_ - from_ - rc
- Variant of `new_client`that works on an`Rc<S>`.
- [new_](https://docs.rs/fn.new_future_client.html)- future_ - client
- Creates a `Client`from a future that resolves to a`Client`.

# capnp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp/^0.26.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#capn-proto-runtime-library)Cap’n Proto Runtime Library

This crate contains basic facilities for reading and writing
[Cap’n Proto](https://capnproto.org) messages in Rust. It is intended to
be used in conjunction with code generated by the
[capnpc-rust](https://crates.io/crates/capnpc) crate.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [any_](https://docs.rs/any_pointer/index.html)- pointer
- Untyped pointer that can be cast to any struct, list, or capability type.
- [any_](https://docs.rs/any_pointer_list/index.html)- pointer_ - list
- List of AnyPointers.
- [capability](https://docs.rs/capability/index.html)
- Hooks for the RPC system.
- [capability_](https://docs.rs/capability_list/index.html)- list
- List of capabilities.
- [constant](https://docs.rs/constant/index.html)
- Helper type for generated Struct and List constants.
- [data](https://docs.rs/data/index.html)
- Sequence of bytes.
- [data_](https://docs.rs/data_list/index.html)- list
- List of sequences of bytes.
- [dynamic_](https://docs.rs/dynamic_list/index.html)- list
- Dynamically-typed lists.
- [dynamic_](https://docs.rs/dynamic_struct/index.html)- struct
- Dynamically-typed structs.
- [dynamic_](https://docs.rs/dynamic_value/index.html)- value
- Dynamically typed values.
- [enum_](https://docs.rs/enum_list/index.html)- list
- List of enums.
- [introspect](https://docs.rs/introspect/index.html)
- Traits and types to support run-time type introspection, i.e. reflection.
- [io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html)
- Custom I/O traits that roughly mirror `std::io::{Read, BufRead, Write}`. This extra layer of indirection enables support of no-std environments.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/list_list/index.html)- list
- List of lists.
- [message](https://docs.rs/message/index.html)
- Untyped root container for a Cap’n Proto value.
- [primitive_](https://docs.rs/primitive_list/index.html)- list
- List of primitives.
- [private](https://docs.rs/private/index.html)
- Implementation details that should never be directly used by clients.
- [raw](https://docs.rs/raw/index.html)
- Functions providing low level access to encoded data.
- [schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)
- Convenience wrappers of the datatypes defined in schema.capnp.
- [schema_](https://docs.rs/schema_capnp/index.html)- capnp
- Code generated from
[schema.capnp](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/master/c%2B%2B/src/capnp/schema.capnp).
- [serialize](https://docs.rs/serialize/index.html)
- Reading and writing of messages using the
[standard stream framing](https://capnproto.org/encoding.html#serialization-over-a-stream).
- [serialize_](https://docs.rs/serialize_packed/index.html)- packed
- Reading and writing of messages using the
[packed stream encoding](https://capnproto.org/encoding.html#packing).
- [struct_](https://docs.rs/struct_list/index.html)- list
- List of structs.
- [text](https://docs.rs/text/index.html)
- UTF-8 encoded text.
- [text_](https://docs.rs/text_list/index.html)- list
- List of strings containing UTF-8 encoded text.
- [traits](https://docs.rs/traits/index.html)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [generated_](https://docs.rs/macro.generated_code.html)- code
- Macro for importing Rust code that has been generated by `capnpc::CompilerCommand`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Describes an arbitrary error that prevented an operation from completing.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.MessageSize.html)- Size
- Size of a message. Every generated struct has a method `.total_size()`that returns this.
- [NotIn](https://docs.rs/struct.NotInSchema.html)- Schema
- An enum value or union discriminant that was not found among those defined in a schema.
- [Word](https://docs.rs/struct.Word.html)
- 8 bytes, aligned to an 8-byte boundary.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorKind.html)- Kind
- The general nature of an error. The purpose of this enum is not to describe the error itself, but rather to describe how the client might want to respond to the error.
- [Output](https://docs.rs/enum.OutputSegments.html)- Segments
- Helper struct that allows `MessageBuilder::get_segments_for_output()`to avoid heap allocations in the single-segment case.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [word](https://docs.rs/fn.word.html)
- Constructs a word with the given bytes.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- Because messages are lazily validated, the return type of any method that reads a pointer field must be wrapped in a Result.

# futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3.0/

## Expand description

Abstractions for asynchronous programming.

This crate provides a number of core abstractions for writing asynchronous code:

- [Futures](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)are single eventual values produced by asynchronous computations. Some programming languages (e.g. JavaScript) call this concept “promise”.
- [Streams](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)represent a series of values produced asynchronously.
- [Sinks](https://docs.rs/sink/index.html)provide support for asynchronous writing of data.
- [Executors](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html)are responsible for running asynchronous tasks.

The crate also contains abstractions for [asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) and
[cross-task communication](https://docs.rs/channel/index.html).

Underlying all of this is the *task system*, which is a form of lightweight
threading. Large asynchronous computations are built up using futures,
streams and sinks, and then spawned as independent tasks that are run to
completion, but *do not block* the thread running them.

The following example describes how the task system context is built and used within macros and keywords such as async and await!.

```
fn main() {
    let pool = ThreadPool::new().expect("Failed to build pool");
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::unbounded::<i32>();
    // Create a future by an async block, where async is responsible for an
    // implementation of Future. At this point no executor has been provided
    // to this future, so it will not be running.
    let fut_values = async {
        // Create another async block, again where the Future implementation
        // is generated by async. Since this is inside of a parent async block,
        // it will be provided with the executor of the parent block when the parent
        // block is executed.
        //
        // This executor chaining is done by Future::poll whose second argument
        // is a std::task::Context. This represents our executor, and the Future
        // implemented by this async block can be polled using the parent async
        // block's executor.
        let fut_tx_result = async move {
            (0..100).for_each(|v| {
                tx.unbounded_send(v).expect("Failed to send");
            })
        };
        // Use the provided thread pool to spawn the generated future
        // responsible for transmission
        pool.spawn_ok(fut_tx_result);
        let fut_values = rx
            .map(|v| v * 2)
            .collect();
        // Use the executor provided to this async block to wait for the
        // future to complete.
        fut_values.await
    };
    // Actually execute the above future, which will invoke Future::poll and
    // subsequently chain appropriate Future::poll and methods needing executors
    // to drive all futures. Eventually fut_values will be driven to completion.
    let values: Vec<i32> = executor::block_on(fut_values);
    println!("Values={:?}", values);
}
```
The majority of examples and code snippets in this crate assume that they are inside an async block as written above.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- Futures-powered synchronization primitives.

- This module contains the `Never`type.

- A “prelude” for crates using the `futures`crate.

- Asynchronous sinks.
- [stream](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)
- Asynchronous streams.
- [task](https://docs.rs/task/index.html)
- Tools for working with tasks.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html)- `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, returning a tuple of all results once complete.
- [pending](https://docs.rs/macro.pending.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which yields to the event loop once.
- [pin_mut](https://docs.rs/macro.pin_mut.html)
- Pins a value on the stack.
- [poll](https://docs.rs/macro.poll.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which returns the result of polling a future once within the
current `async`context.
- [ready](https://docs.rs/macro.ready.html)
- Extracts the successful type of `Poll<T>`.
- [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html)- `async-await`and- `std`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. If multiple futures are ready,
one will be pseudo-randomly selected at runtime. Futures directly
passed to `select!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/macro.select_biased.html)- biased - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. Unlike `select!``select_biased!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/macro.stream_select.html)- select - `async-await`and- `std`
- Combines several streams, all producing the same `Item`type, into one stream. This is similar to`select_all`but does not require the streams to all be the same type. It also keeps the streams inline, and does not require`Box<dyn Stream>`s to be allocated. Streams passed to this macro must be`Unpin`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html)- join - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, resolving to a `Result`

---

# capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnp-rpc/latest/target-redirect/capnp_rpc/

## Expand description

An implementation of the [Cap’n Proto remote procedure call](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html)
protocol. Includes all [Level 1](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#protocol-features) features.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
# Cap'n Proto schema
interface Foo {
    identity @0 (x: UInt32) -> (y: UInt32);
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Rust server defining an implementation of Foo.
struct FooImpl;
impl foo::Server for FooImpl {
    async fn identity(
        self: Rc<Self>,
        params: foo::IdentityParams,
        mut results: foo::IdentityResults
    ) -> Result<(), ::capnp::Error> {
        let x = params.get()?.get_x();
        results.get().set_y(x);
        Ok(())
    }
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Rust client calling a remote implementation of Foo.
let mut request = foo_client.identity_request();
request.get().set_x(123);
let promise = request.send().promise.and_then(|response| {
    println!("results = {}", response.get()?.get_y());
    Ok(())
});
```
For a more complete example, see [https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator)

- [Connection](https://docs.rs/trait.Connection.html)
- A two-way RPC connection.
- [Flow](https://docs.rs/trait.FlowController.html)- Controller
- Tracks a particular RPC stream in order to implement a flow control algorithm.
- [Incoming](https://docs.rs/trait.IncomingMessage.html)- Message
- A message received from a `VatNetwork`
- [Outgoing](https://docs.rs/trait.OutgoingMessage.html)- Message
- A message to be sent by a `VatNetwork`
- [SetTarget](https://docs.rs/trait.SetTarget.html)
- Trait implemented by the reconnecting client to set new connection out-of-band.
- [VatNetwork](https://docs.rs/trait.VatNetwork.html)
- Network facility between vats, it determines how to form connections between vats.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [auto_](https://docs.rs/fn.auto_reconnect.html)- reconnect
- Creates a new client that reconnects when getting `ErrorKind::Disconnected`
- [lazy_](https://docs.rs/fn.lazy_auto_reconnect.html)- auto_ - reconnect
- Creates a new client that lazily connect and also reconnects when getting `ErrorKind::Disconnected`
- [new_](https://docs.rs/fn.new_client.html)- client
- Creates a new local RPC client of type `C`out of an object that implements a server trait`S`.
- [new_](https://docs.rs/fn.new_client_from_rc.html)- client_ - from_ - rc
- Variant of `new_client`that works on an`Rc<S>`.
- [new_](https://docs.rs/fn.new_future_client.html)- future_ - client
- Creates a `Client`from a future that resolves to a`Client`.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

}## Expand description

The general nature of an error. The purpose of this enum is not to describe the error itself, but rather to describe how the client might want to respond to the error.

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Failed)

### Failed

Something went wrong

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Overloaded)

### Overloaded

The call failed because of a temporary lack of resources. This could be space resources (out of memory, out of disk space) or time resources (request queue overflow, operation timed out).

The operation might work if tried again, but it should NOT be repeated immediately as this may simply exacerbate the problem.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Disconnected)

### Disconnected

The call required communication over a connection that has been lost. The caller will need to re-establish connections and try again.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Unimplemented)

### Unimplemented

The requested method is not implemented. The caller may wish to revert to a fallback approach based on other methods.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.BufferNotLargeEnough)

### BufferNotLargeEnough

Buffer is not large enough

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CannotCreateACanonicalMessageWithACapability)

### CannotCreateACanonicalMessageWithACapability

Cannot create a canonical message with a capability

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CannotSetAnyPointerFieldToAPrimitiveValue)

### CannotSetAnyPointerFieldToAPrimitiveValue

Cannot set AnyPointer field to a primitive value

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CantHandleNonStructInlineComposite)

### CantHandleNonStructInlineComposite

Don’t know how to handle non-STRUCT inline composite.

### EmptyBuffer

Empty buffer

### EmptySlice

Empty slice

# mirx - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mirx/0.39.0/mirx/

On-disk discriminants are byte-stable once shipped. Naming and byte-order
match mirui::ColorFormat so reader output is zero-copy on the mirui side.
Discriminants are partitioned by family: byte >> 4 identifies the family
(1 = indexed, 2 = alpha-only, 3 = luma, 4 = RGB565, 5 = RGB888, 6 = 32-bit),
leaving the rest of each 16-byte run open for same-family extensions.

Single-chunk file with an arbitrary chunk_type and a raw payload.
FONT / VECTOR / custom critical chunks all wrap their format-specific
header inside payload. The primary header fields (color_format,
width, height, stride) are zeroed because they don’t apply.

Multi-chunk file: writes chunks (each (chunk_type, flags, payload)) into one CHUNK-layout buffer, table then payloads. The
reader resolves them via ChunkFile::chunk_payload /
ChunkFile::chunk_payloads. Primary header fields stay zeroed —
a multi-chunk file (e.g. several FONT representations) has no single
primary. encode_chunk_generic is the one-chunk special case.

---

# everruns_integrations_e2b - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-integrations-e2b/0.17.3/everruns_integrations_e2b/

## Expand description

E2B cloud sandboxes for Everruns agents.

`everruns-integrations-e2b` is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com)
ecosystem. It gives agents cloud sandboxes backed by [E2B](https://e2b.dev),
so they can create isolated environments, run processes, and read or write
files without touching the host. Sandboxes are managed per session with
leased-resource cleanup, and authenticate with a user-supplied E2B API key.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_core::capabilities::Capability;
use everruns_integrations_e2b::E2BCapability;
let capability = E2BCapability;
assert_eq!(capability.id(), "e2b");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#design-notes)Design notes

- External integration crate, auto-registered via the inventory plugin system.
- Bring-your-own API-key connection model: credentials resolve from the user
connection only and fail with `ConnectionRequired`if not configured.
- Session-scoped sandbox state with leased-resource cleanup, similar to Daytona.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [client](https://docs.rs/client/index.html)
- E2B API client.
- [connection](https://docs.rs/connection/index.html)
- [state](https://docs.rs/state/index.html)
- E2B API types and session state helpers.

---

# everruns_integrations_daytona - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-integrations-daytona/0.17.3/everruns_integrations_daytona/

## Expand description

Daytona cloud sandboxes for Everruns agents.

`everruns-integrations-daytona` is part of the
[Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem. It adds cloud-based sandboxed
code execution backed by the [Daytona](https://www.daytona.io) REST API,
letting agents create sandboxes, run commands with streamed output, and read
or write files inside an isolated environment. Sandboxes are managed per
session and authenticated with a user-supplied Daytona API key.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_core::capabilities::Capability;
use everruns_integrations_daytona::DaytonaCapability;
let capability = DaytonaCapability;
assert_eq!(capability.id(), "daytona");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#design-notes)Design notes

- External integration crate, auto-registered via the inventory plugin system.
- State (API key + per-sandbox connection info) lives in the secrets store.
- Two-tier Daytona API: Management API for lifecycle, Toolbox API for in-sandbox operations.
- All execution goes through the Session API (`/process/session`) using a shared session, async execution, and log polling for real-time streaming output.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [client](https://docs.rs/client/index.html)
- Daytona API client and URL encoding utilities.
- [connection](https://docs.rs/connection/index.html)
- [openapi_](https://docs.rs/openapi_spec/index.html)- spec
- Embedded Daytona OpenAPI specification for the API calling feature.
- [state](https://docs.rs/state/index.html)
- Daytona API types and session state management.

---

# everruns_integrations_github - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-integrations-github/0.17.3/everruns_integrations_github/

## Expand description

GitHub-backed blueprints for Everruns.

This crate registers the `github_scout` capability through Everruns’ inventory
plugin system. The capability is blueprint-only: it does not add tools to a
host agent, and instead contributes the `github_scout` agent blueprint.

`github_scout` runs as a read-only child agent with private GitHub REST API
tools for code search, file reads, and issue or pull request search. Tool
credentials are resolved from the existing `github` user connection, with a
`GITHUB_TOKEN` session secret fallback for local and compatibility flows.

---

# ferrocat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferrocat/2.1.0/ferrocat/

## Expand description

Public Rust entry point for the `ferrocat` workspace.

This crate re-exports the primary API surface from the lower-level
`ferrocat-po` and `ferrocat-icu` crates so application code can depend on a
single package.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

The default feature set is `full`, which enables the complete current API
surface through `catalog` and `serde`.

- `catalog`exposes high-level catalog parsing, updates, combining, audits, machine-translation metadata, plural handling, FCL storage, and runtime artifact compilation.
- `serde`enables serde support in the re-exported- `ferrocat-po`and- `ferrocat-icu`types.
- `compile`,- `mt`, and- `plurals`are reserved subsystem aliases. Today they imply- `catalog`; they do not reduce or split the catalog API surface.

Use `default-features = false` for low-level PO and ICU parsing without the
catalog layer. Enabling `compile`, `mt`, or `plurals` currently has the same
dependency effect as enabling `catalog`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use ferrocat::{icu, po};
let po = po::parse_po("msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hallo\"\n")?;
let icu = icu::parse_icu("Hello {name}")?;
assert_eq!(po.items[0].msgid, "Hello");
assert_eq!(icu.nodes.len(), 2);
```
```
use ferrocat::catalog::{
    CompileSelectedCatalogArtifactOptions, CompiledCatalogIdIndex, CompiledKeyStrategy,
    ParseCatalogOptions, compile_catalog_artifact_selected, parse_catalog,
};
let source = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hello\"\n", "en").with_locale("en"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let requested = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hallo\"\n", "en").with_locale("de"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let index = CompiledCatalogIdIndex::new(&[&requested, &source], CompiledKeyStrategy::FerrocatV1)?;
let compiled_ids = index.iter().map(|(id, _)| id).collect::<Vec<_>>();
let compiled = compile_catalog_artifact_selected(
    &[&requested, &source],
    &index,
    &CompileSelectedCatalogArtifactOptions::new("de", "en", &compiled_ids),
)?;
assert_eq!(compiled.messages.len(), 1);
```
```
use ferrocat::catalog::{
    CatalogAuditOptions, ParseCatalogOptions, audit_catalogs, parse_catalog,
};
let source = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Checkout\"\nmsgstr \"Checkout\"\n", "en").with_locale("en"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let target = parse_catalog(ParseCatalogOptions::new("", "en").with_locale("de"))?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let report = audit_catalogs(&[&source, &target], &CatalogAuditOptions::new("en"))?;
assert!(report.has_errors());
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [catalog](https://docs.rs/catalog/index.html)- `catalog`
- High-level catalog maintenance, audit, and runtime artifact APIs.
- [icu](https://docs.rs/icu/index.html)
- ICU MessageFormat parsing, analysis, compatibility, and metadata APIs.
- [po](https://docs.rs/po/index.html)
- Low-level PO parsing, serialization, and text merge APIs.

# zeros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/zeros/20.0.0/zeros/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#zeros)Zeros

[§](https://docs.rs#project)Project

- License: GNU Lesser General Public License, either version 3, or (at your option) any later version.
- *This project follows*- [Semantic Versioning 2.0.0](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

This project provides:

- *Some*- [hash functions](https://docs.rs/keccak/index.html)from- [Keccak](https://keccak.team).
- Some cryptographic implementations: [Chacha](https://docs.rs/chacha/index.html),[Poly1305](https://docs.rs/poly1305/index.html),[Argon2](https://docs.rs/argon2/index.html)…

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

- Currently only little-endian systems are supported. We don’t have access or knowledge to test on big-endian systems.
- Internal state stores data on `u64``u64`natively.
- Accuracy/correctness is highest priority. Speed is second. Currently, it’s slower than well-known implementations, such as
[OpenSSL](https://www.openssl.org).
- Documentation is built with all features. Some of them are optional. If you see components from other crates, you can view source to see what features are required.
- Night Rust is required to build.

[§](https://docs.rs#async-support-understanding-your-responsibilities)Async Support: Understanding Your Responsibilities

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

This crate provides optional async support for cryptographic operations via the `tokio` feature flag. When enabled, it offers
`AsyncRead`/`AsyncWrite` implementations that integrate with the [ tokio](https://docs.rs/tokio) async runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#important-performance-and-runtime-considerations)Important: Performance and Runtime Considerations

**Cryptographic operations are CPU-bound tasks.** Unlike I/O operations that naturally yield control during waiting periods, cryptographic
functions perform continuous computation without internal await points.

When using this crate’s async API, **you are responsible for managing the balance between computational work and runtime responsiveness.**

[§](https://docs.rs#why-this-matters)Why This Matters

Async runtimes use cooperative scheduling. Tasks are expected to yield control periodically to allow other tasks to make progress. If a single task runs a CPU-intensive operation for too long without yielding, it can:

- Starve other tasks waiting to run
- Delay I/O event processing
- Create noticeable latency spikes
- Potentially deadlock the runtime in extreme cases

[§](https://docs.rs#the-chunk-size-principle)The Chunk Size Principle

The core guideline is: **ensure each chunk of data processed in a single operation is small enough that the cryptographic work completes
within a reasonable time frame for your runtime.**

For example, when calling `write_all()` or `read_exact()` on async streams from this crate:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// ❌ Potentially problematic: Processing 1GB in one call
async_writer.write_all(&huge_data[..]).await?;
// ✅ Better: Process in manageable chunks
for chunk in huge_data.chunks(8 * 1024) {
    async_writer.write_all(chunk).await?;
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#general-guidance)General Guidance

While specific time limits depend on your runtime and hardware, consider these principles:

[§](https://docs.rs#1--runtime-budgets)1.  Runtime budgets

Most async runtimes expect tasks to yield every few hundred microseconds of CPU time. If your chunks are large enough that cryptographic processing exceeds this, you risk starvation.

[§](https://docs.rs#2--test-with-your-workload)2.  **Test with your workload**

The appropriate chunk size depends on:

- Your CPU speed
- The specific cryptographic operation (SHA-3 is slower than Poly1305-ChaCha20)
- Your runtime’s scheduler behavior
- Your application’s latency requirements

[§](https://docs.rs#3--when-in-doubt-use-smaller-chunks)3.  **When in doubt, use smaller chunks**

Processing in smaller chunks (e.g., 8-64 KB) is almost always safer than processing large blocks.

[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-using-blocking-threads)Alternative: Using Blocking Threads

If you need to process large amounts of data and cannot or don’t want to manage chunk sizes, consider using the synchronous API on a blocking thread:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Using tokio as an example, but similar patterns exist for other runtimes
tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || {
    // Use the standard Read/Write API here
    hasher.write_all(&large_data)?;
    let result = hasher.finish();
    // ...
}).await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#what-this-crate-does-not-guarantee)What This Crate Does Not Guarantee

The async API provided by this crate is designed to:

- Follow the `AsyncRead`/`AsyncWrite`contract
- Be compatible with async runtime event loops
- Process data correctly regardless of chunk size

However, it does **not** and **cannot** guarantee:

- That your operation will run within any specific time limit
- That the runtime will remain responsive regardless of how you use it
- Automatic chunking or yield insertion

**These are your responsibility as the user.**

[§](https://docs.rs#understanding-the-trade-off)Understanding the Trade-off

When you enable the `tokio` feature and use this crate’s async API, you are choosing a programming style (async/await) over manual thread
management. This choice gives you better ergonomics and scalability – but with the trade-off that you must be mindful of how long your
tasks run.

This is similar to writing any CPU-intensive operation in an async context: the runtime provides the tools, but you provide the discipline.

[§](https://docs.rs#summary)Summary

[§](https://docs.rs#-do)✅ Do:

- Process data in reasonably sized chunks
- Test your application’s performance under load
- Use blocking threads for truly large operations
- Monitor task latency in production

[§](https://docs.rs#-avoid)❌ Avoid:

- Processing extremely large buffers in single async operations
- Assuming that “async” makes CPU work free
- Ignoring runtime responsiveness in your performance testing

*Remember: The async support in this crate is about programming style and API compatibility. The responsibility for runtime behavior lies
with you, the user.*

# everruns_integrations_duckduckgo - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-integrations-duckduckgo/0.17.3/everruns_integrations_duckduckgo/

## Expand description

DuckDuckGo Instant Answer integration for Everruns.

Instant answers via DuckDuckGo Instant Answer API.
Provides `duckduckgo_search` tool for agents to get instant answers,
abstracts, related topics, and definitions.

This crate is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_core::capabilities::Capability;
use everruns_integrations_duckduckgo::DuckDuckGoCapability;
let capability = DuckDuckGoCapability;
assert_eq!(capability.id(), "duckduckgo");
assert_eq!(capability.tools().len(), 1);
```
Decision: External integration crate, auto-registered via inventory plugin system Decision: No API key required — DuckDuckGo Instant Answer API is free Decision: Stateless — no per-resource state management needed

# ferrocat_po - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferrocat-po/2.1.0/ferrocat_po/

## Expand description

Performance-first PO parsing and serialization.

The crate exposes both owned and borrowed parsers for gettext PO files, a byte-oriented UTF-8 parser entry point, plus helpers for serialization and higher-level catalog update workflows.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

The default feature set is `full`, which currently enables the `catalog`
workflow layer.

- `catalog`exposes high-level catalog parsing, updates, combining, audits, machine-translation metadata, plural handling, FCL storage, and runtime artifact compilation. It also enables the catalog-layer dependencies used for hashing, atomic file updates, serde JSON output, ICU diagnostics, and CLDR plural data.
- `serde`enables serde implementations for low-level PO document types and is also enabled by- `catalog`for catalog-layer JSON/report shapes.
- `compile`,- `mt`, and- `plurals`are reserved subsystem aliases. Today they imply- `catalog`; they do not reduce or split the catalog API surface.

Use `default-features = false` for the low-level PO parser, borrowed parser,
serializer, string helpers, and lightweight `merge_catalog` helper without
catalog-layer dependencies. Enabling `compile`, `mt`, or `plurals` currently
has the same dependency effect as enabling `catalog`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use ferrocat_po::{PoFile, SerializeOptions, parse_po, stringify_po};
let input = "msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hallo\"\n";
let file = parse_po(input)?;
assert_eq!(file.items[0].msgid, "Hello");
let output = stringify_po(&file, &SerializeOptions::default());
assert!(output.contains("msgid \"Hello\""));
```
```
use ferrocat_po::parse_po_bytes;
let input = b"msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hallo\"\n";
let file = parse_po_bytes(input)?;
assert_eq!(file.items[0].msgstr[0], "Hallo");
```
```
use ferrocat_po::{
    CompileCatalogArtifactOptions, CompileSelectedCatalogArtifactOptions,
    CompiledCatalogIdIndex, ParseCatalogOptions, compile_catalog_artifact_selected,
    parse_catalog,
};
let source = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hello\"\n", "en").with_locale("en"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let requested = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Hello\"\nmsgstr \"Hallo\"\n", "en").with_locale("de"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let index = CompiledCatalogIdIndex::new(&[&requested, &source], ferrocat_po::CompiledKeyStrategy::FerrocatV1)?;
let compiled_ids = index.iter().map(|(id, _)| id).collect::<Vec<_>>();
let compiled = compile_catalog_artifact_selected(
    &[&requested, &source],
    &index,
    &CompileSelectedCatalogArtifactOptions::new("de", "en", &compiled_ids),
)?;
assert_eq!(compiled.messages.len(), 1);
```
```
use ferrocat_po::{CatalogAuditOptions, ParseCatalogOptions, audit_catalogs, parse_catalog};
let source = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Hello {name}\"\nmsgstr \"Hello {name}\"\n", "en")
        .with_locale("en"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let target = parse_catalog(
    ParseCatalogOptions::new("msgid \"Hello {name}\"\nmsgstr \"Hallo\"\n", "en")
        .with_locale("de"),
)?
.into_normalized_view()?;
let report = audit_catalogs(&[&source, &target], &CatalogAuditOptions::new("en"))?;
assert!(report.has_errors());
```

# shikumi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/shikumi/0.1.129/shikumi/

## Expand description

Shikumi (仕組み) — config discovery, hot-reload, and `ArcSwap` store
for Nix-managed desktop applications.

Extracted from [karakuri](https://github.com/pleme-io/karakuri)’s configuration
system, shikumi provides the shared infrastructure for desktop apps that need:

- **XDG config discovery**with env var overrides and format preference
- **Figment provider chains**(defaults → env vars → config file)
- **Lock-free concurrent reads**via- `ArcSwap`
- **Hot-reload**with symlink-aware file watching (for nix-darwin managed configs)

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use serde::Deserialize;
use shikumi::{ConfigDiscovery, ConfigStore, Format};
#[derive(Deserialize, Clone, Debug, Default)]
struct MyConfig {
    window_width: Option<u32>,
}
let path = ConfigDiscovery::new("myapp")
    .env_override("MYAPP_CONFIG")
    .formats(&[Format::Yaml, Format::Toml])
    .discover()
    .expect("config file not found");
let store = ConfigStore::<MyConfig>::load(&path, "MYAPP_")
    .expect("failed to load config");
let config = store.get();
println!("width: {:?}", config.window_width);
```

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [coverage](https://docs.rs/coverage/index.html)

- The **discovered-defaults tier**— environment-discovered layered defaults, merged into a config chain*above*the developer’s prescribed defaults but*below*operator file/env config.
- [macros](https://docs.rs/macros/index.html)
- Declarative macros over the closed-axis / product-cube / tiered-config
discipline — `perm_cube!`and`tiered_permutation_test!`.
- [nix_](https://docs.rs/nix_provider/index.html)- provider
- Figment provider for Nix expression configs.
- [secret](https://docs.rs/secret/index.html)
- Secret resolution for config fields that reference external vaults.
- [secret_](https://docs.rs/secret_client/index.html)- client
- Unified secret-client abstraction.
- [tiered](https://docs.rs/tiered/index.html)
- Tiered configuration — **the shikumi configuration prime directive**.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [closed_](https://docs.rs/macro.closed_axis_label_string_surface.html)- axis_ - label_ - string_ - surface
- Emit the canonical `(Display, FromStr, Serialize, Deserialize)`string-surface quartet for a`crate::ClosedAxisLabel`
- [closed_](https://docs.rs/macro.closed_axis_label_string_surface_typed_err.html)- axis_ - label_ - string_ - surface_ - typed_ - err
- Emit the canonical
`(Display, FromStr, Serialize, Deserialize)`string-surface quartet for a closed-axis-label primitive whose`FromStr::Err`is a bespoke typed label-carrying error struct — the sibling lift of`closed_axis_label_string_surface!``crate::ModalityClass``crate::SupportCardinalityClass``crate::SupportBoundaryDistance``crate::SupportMagnitudeDirection``crate::PartitionFace``Result<_, _>`shape rather than the`crate::ShikumiError::Parse``closed_axis_label_string_surface!`
- [perm_](https://docs.rs/macro.perm_cube.html)- cube
- Mechanically emit a `crate::ProductCube``crate::ClosedAxis``const ALL`(full Cartesian product) +`impl ClosedAxis`+`impl ProductCube`.
- [serde_](https://docs.rs/macro.serde_via_display_fromstr.html)- via_ - display_ - fromstr
- Emit the canonical `(Serialize, Deserialize)`serde pair for any type whose canonical scalar form is its`std::fmt::Display``std::str::FromStr`
- [tiered_](https://docs.rs/macro.tiered_permutation_test.html)- permutation_ - test
- Emit ONE matrix `#[test]`that stamps every cube cell onto every config tier, serde-round-trips each, runs a user`apply`closure, and aggregates EVERY failure before asserting.

# ferrocat_icu - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferrocat-icu/2.1.0/ferrocat_icu/

## Expand description

Compact, performance-oriented ICU `MessageFormat` parsing primitives.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use ferrocat_icu::{extract_variables, parse_icu};
let message = parse_icu("Hello {name}, you have {count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}}.")?;
assert_eq!(extract_variables(&message), vec!["name", "count"]);
```
```
use ferrocat_icu::{
    IcuCompatibilityOptions, analyze_icu, compare_icu_messages, parse_icu,
};
let source = parse_icu("Hello {name}, you have {count, number, integer} files.")?;
let translation = parse_icu("Hallo, du hast {count, number, integer} Dateien.")?;
let source_analysis = analyze_icu(&source);
assert_eq!(source_analysis.arguments.len(), 2);
let report = compare_icu_messages(
    &source,
    &translation,
    &IcuCompatibilityOptions::default(),
);
assert!(report.has_errors());
```
```
use ferrocat_icu::{
    MessageArgumentKind, MessageMetadataInput, normalize_message_metadata,
};
let metadata = normalize_message_metadata(MessageMetadataInput::new(
    "{count, plural, one {One item} other {# items}}",
))?;
assert_eq!(
    metadata.args.get("count").map(|argument| argument.kind),
    Some(MessageArgumentKind::Number)
);
assert!(metadata.selectors.contains_key("count"));
```
```
use ferrocat_icu::{parse_icu, stringify_icu};
let parsed = parse_icu("Hello {name}")?;
assert_eq!(stringify_icu(&parsed), "Hello {name}");
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [diagnostic_](https://docs.rs/diagnostic_codes/index.html)- codes
- Stable machine-readable diagnostic codes emitted by `ferrocat-icu`.

# everruns_gemini - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-gemini/0.17.3/everruns_gemini/

## Expand description

Google Gemini LLM provider driver for Everruns.

`everruns-gemini` is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem.
It implements the `ChatDriver` contract from `everruns-core`, so the agent
loop can run against Google’s Gemini API, and registers itself through
[ register_driver](https://docs.rs/fn.register_driver.html).

Core has no knowledge of specific providers; hosts register whichever drivers
they want available via `register_driver` at startup.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_gemini::register_driver;
use everruns_core::DriverRegistry;
let mut registry = DriverRegistry::new();
register_driver(&mut registry);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Driver](https://docs.rs/struct.DriverRegistry.html)- Registry
- Registry for LLM drivers
- [Gemini](https://docs.rs/struct.GeminiChatDriver.html)- Chat - Driver
- Google Gemini Chat Driver

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Chat](https://docs.rs/trait.ChatDriver.html)- Driver
- Trait for LLM drivers

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [register_](https://docs.rs/fn.register_driver.html)- driver
- Register the Gemini driver with the driver registry

---

# everruns_bedrock - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-bedrock/0.17.3/everruns_bedrock/

## Expand description

AWS Bedrock Runtime provider driver for Everruns.

`everruns-bedrock` implements the [ ChatDriver](https://docs.rs/trait.ChatDriver.html) contract from

`everruns-core`
using the AWS Bedrock Runtime `ConverseStream` API.Credentials are encoded as JSON in the `api_key` field:

`{"access_key_id":"...","secret_access_key":"...","session_token":"...","region":"us-east-1"}``session_token` is optional. The `base_url` field is unused.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_bedrock::{BedrockChatDriver, register_driver};
use everruns_core::DriverRegistry;
let mut registry = DriverRegistry::new();
register_driver(&mut registry);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Bedrock](https://docs.rs/struct.BedrockChatDriver.html)- Chat - Driver
- AWS Bedrock Runtime Chat Driver.
- [Driver](https://docs.rs/struct.DriverRegistry.html)- Registry
- Registry for LLM drivers

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Chat](https://docs.rs/trait.ChatDriver.html)- Driver
- Trait for LLM drivers

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [register_](https://docs.rs/fn.register_driver.html)- driver
- Register the Bedrock driver with the given registry.

# azalea_reflection_proxy - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/azalea-reflection-proxy/0.1.1/azalea_reflection_proxy/

## Expand description

azalea-reflection-proxy — spectate and control an azalea bot session through a local reflection proxy. Rust port of aesthetic0001/mineflayer-reflection-proxy.

The proxy owns the single real (Microsoft-authed) connection to the
target server. Your bot connects to the proxy locally as an offline
client and becomes the controller; vanilla clients that join the
same local address become spectators, see the bot as a live player
entity, and can take over with `,acquire`.

```
use azalea_reflection_proxy::ReflectionProxy;
let proxy = ReflectionProxy::builder()
    .target("mc.hypixel.net")
    .email("you@example.com")
    .spawn()
    .await?;
// then point your azalea bot at it instead of the real server:
//   ClientBuilder::new()
//       .set_handler(handle)
//       .start(Account::offline("reflected"), proxy.local_addr())
// and add a vanilla-client server entry for the same address to
// spectate. proxy.local_addr() is a real SocketAddr, so a bound
// port of 0 picks a free one.
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use plugin::`- [Frame](https://docs.rs/plugin/struct.Frame.html);
- `pub use plugin::`- [Pipeline](https://docs.rs/plugin/struct.Pipeline.html);
- `pub use plugin::`- [ProxyPlugin](https://docs.rs/plugin/trait.ProxyPlugin.html);
- `pub use plugin::`- [Verdict](https://docs.rs/plugin/enum.Verdict.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [plugin](https://docs.rs/plugin/index.html)
- Plugin pipeline — the azalea equivalent of the JS project’s plugin system (anonymize / snapshot / synchronization / inventory / replicator).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Proxy](https://docs.rs/struct.ProxyBuilder.html)- Builder
- Configuration for a reflection proxy. Build with
`ReflectionProxy::builder`
- [Reflection](https://docs.rs/struct.ReflectionProxy.html)- Proxy
- A running reflection proxy. Dropping the handle does NOT stop it;
call `Self::shutdown`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Proxy](https://docs.rs/enum.ProxyEvent.html)- Event
- Things happening inside the proxy that the host program may care
about — the port of the original’s `clientJoin`/`changeControl`server events. Subscribe with`ReflectionProxy::subscribe`

# everruns_openrouter - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-openrouter/0.17.3/everruns_openrouter/

## Expand description

OpenRouter provider driver for Everruns.

`everruns-openrouter` is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com)
ecosystem. It implements the [ ChatDriver](https://docs.rs/trait.ChatDriver.html) contract from

`everruns-core`
and registers the OpenRouter provider into a [.](https://docs.rs/struct.DriverRegistry.html)

`DriverRegistry`OpenRouter exposes an OpenAI-compatible Responses API, so [ OpenRouterChatDriver](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterChatDriver.html)
wraps

`everruns_core::OpenResponsesProtocolChatDriver` tagged with
`DriverId::OpenRouter`. Its `/models` endpoint advertises richer metadata
(a `supported_parameters` array) that the crate parses into capability
profiles at discovery time.[§](https://docs.rs#registering-the-driver)Registering the Driver

```
use everruns_core::DriverRegistry;
use everruns_openrouter::register_driver;
let mut registry = DriverRegistry::new();
register_driver(&mut registry);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Driver](https://docs.rs/struct.DriverRegistry.html)- Registry
- Registry for LLM drivers
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterArchitecture.html)- Router - Architecture
- Modality metadata from OpenRouter’s `architecture`object.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterChatDriver.html)- Router - Chat - Driver
- OpenRouter driver using its OpenAI-compatible Responses API.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterModelInfo.html)- Router - Model - Info
- Individual model entry from OpenRouter’s models API.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterModelsResponse.html)- Router - Models - Response
- Response from OpenRouter’s `/api/v1/models`endpoint.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterPricing.html)- Router - Pricing
- Per-token pricing reported by OpenRouter’s `pricing`object.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterRequestExtension.html)- Router - Request - Extension
- Layers OpenRouter-specific fields onto an Open Responses request body.
- [Open](https://docs.rs/struct.OpenRouterTopProvider.html)- Router - TopProvider
- Per-request limits reported by the routed upstream provider.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Chat](https://docs.rs/trait.ChatDriver.html)- Driver
- Trait for LLM drivers

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [register_](https://docs.rs/fn.register_driver.html)- driver
- Register the OpenRouter driver with the driver registry.

# capnp-rpc 0.26.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnp-rpc/0.26.1

# capnp-rpc-rust

This is a [level one](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#protocol-features)
implementation of the Cap'n Proto remote procedure call protocol.
It is a fairly direct translation of the original
[C++ implementation](https://github.com/sandstorm-io/capnproto).

## Defining an interface

First, make sure that the
[ capnp executable](https://capnproto.org/capnp-tool.html)
is installed on your system,
and that you have the

[crate in the](https://crates.io/crates/capnpc)

`capnpc``build-dependencies` section of your `Cargo.toml`.
Then, in a file named `foo.capnp`, define your interface:```
@0xa7ed6c5c8a98ca40;
interface Bar {
    baz @0 (x :Int32) -> (y :Int32);
}
interface Qux {
    quux @0 (bar :Bar) -> (y :Int32);
}
```
Now you can invoke the schema compiler in a
[ build.rs](http://doc.crates.io/build-script.html) file, like this:

```
```
Such a command generates a `foo_capnp.rs` file in the `OUT_DIR`
directory provided by `cargo`.

To import the generated code, add a line like this at the root of your crate:

`generated_code!`(If you want to import the code at a non-toplevel module location, then you will
need to use the `$Rust.parentModule` annotation, defined in `rust.capnp`.)

## Calling methods on an RPC object

For each defined interface, the generated code includes a `Client` struct
that can be used to call the interface's methods. For example, the following
code calls the `Bar.baz()` method:

```
```
A `bar::Client` is a reference to a possibly-remote `Bar` object.
The Cap'n Proto RPC runtime tracks the number of such references
that are live at any given time and automatically drops the
object when none are left.

## Implementing an interface

The generated code also includes a `Server` trait for each of your interfaces.
To create an RPC-enabled object, you must implement that trait.

```
```
Then you can convert your object into a capability client like this:

```
let client: Client = new_client;
```
This new `client` can now be sent across the network.
You can use it as the bootstrap capability when you construct an `RpcSystem`,
and you can pass it in RPC method arguments and results.

## Async methods

The methods of the generated `Server` traits return
a value of type `impl Future<Output = Result<(), ::capnp::Error>>`.
As you have seen above,
these can be implented as `async fn` methods returning `Result<(), ::capnp::Error>`.

The RPC response will be sent back to the method's caller once two things have happened:

- The `Results`struct has been dropped.
- The method's returned `Future`has resolved.

Usually (1) happens before (2).

Here's an example of a method implementation that does not return immediately because it awaits another request:

```
```
It's possible for multiple calls of `quux()` to be active at the same time
on the same object, and they do not need to return in the same order
as they were called.

## Further reading

- The [hello world example](https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/examples/hello-world)demonstrates a basic request/reply pattern.
- The [calculator example](https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator)demonstrates how to use[promise pipelining](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#time-travel-promise-pipelining).
- The [pubsub example](https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/examples/pubsub)shows how even an interface with no methods can be useful.
- The [Sandstorm raw API example app](https://github.com/dwrensha/sandstorm-rawapi-example-rust)shows how Sandstorm lets you write web apps using Cap'n Proto instead of HTTP.

---

# capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/target-redirect/capnp_rpc/

## Expand description

An implementation of the [Cap’n Proto remote procedure call](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html)
protocol. Includes all [Level 1](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#protocol-features) features.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
# Cap'n Proto schema
interface Foo {
    identity @0 (x: UInt32) -> (y: UInt32);
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Rust server defining an implementation of Foo.
struct FooImpl;
impl foo::Server for FooImpl {
    async fn identity(
        self: Rc<Self>,
        params: foo::IdentityParams,
        mut results: foo::IdentityResults
    ) -> Result<(), ::capnp::Error> {
        let x = params.get()?.get_x();
        results.get().set_y(x);
        Ok(())
    }
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Rust client calling a remote implementation of Foo.
let mut request = foo_client.identity_request();
request.get().set_x(123);
let promise = request.send().promise.and_then(|response| {
    println!("results = {}", response.get()?.get_y());
    Ok(())
});
```
For a more complete example, see [https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [rpc_](https://docs.rs/rpc_capnp/index.html)- capnp
- Code generated from
[rpc.capnp](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/master/c%2B%2B/src/capnp/rpc.capnp).
- [rpc_](https://docs.rs/rpc_twoparty_capnp/index.html)- twoparty_ - capnp
- Code generated from
[rpc-twoparty.capnp](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/master/c%2B%2B/src/capnp/rpc-twoparty.capnp).
- [twoparty](https://docs.rs/twoparty/index.html)
- An implementation of `VatNetwork`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [pry](https://docs.rs/macro.pry.html)
- Like `try!()``Promise<T, E>``Result<T, E>`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Capability](https://docs.rs/struct.CapabilityServerSet.html)- Server - Set
- Collection of unwrappable capabilities.
- [Disconnector](https://docs.rs/struct.Disconnector.html)
- A `Future`that can be run to disconnect an`RpcSystem`’s ConnectionState and wait for it to be closed.
- [Imbued](https://docs.rs/struct.ImbuedMessageBuilder.html)- Message - Builder
- [RpcSystem](https://docs.rs/struct.RpcSystem.html)
- A portal to objects available on the network.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Connection](https://docs.rs/trait.Connection.html)
- A two-way RPC connection.
- [Flow](https://docs.rs/trait.FlowController.html)- Controller
- Tracks a particular RPC stream in order to implement a flow control algorithm.
- [Incoming](https://docs.rs/trait.IncomingMessage.html)- Message
- A message received from a `VatNetwork`
- [Outgoing](https://docs.rs/trait.OutgoingMessage.html)- Message
- A message to be sent by a `VatNetwork`
- [SetTarget](https://docs.rs/trait.SetTarget.html)
- Trait implemented by the reconnecting client to set new connection out-of-band.
- [VatNetwork](https://docs.rs/trait.VatNetwork.html)
- Network facility between vats, it determines how to form connections between vats.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [auto_](https://docs.rs/fn.auto_reconnect.html)- reconnect
- Creates a new client that reconnects when getting `ErrorKind::Disconnected`
- [lazy_](https://docs.rs/fn.lazy_auto_reconnect.html)- auto_ - reconnect
- Creates a new client that lazily connect and also reconnects when getting `ErrorKind::Disconnected`
- [new_](https://docs.rs/fn.new_client.html)- client
- Creates a new local RPC client of type `C`out of an object that implements a server trait`S`.
- [new_](https://docs.rs/fn.new_client_from_rc.html)- client_ - from_ - rc
- Variant of `new_client`that works on an`Rc<S>`.
- [new_](https://docs.rs/fn.new_future_client.html)- future_ - client
- Creates a `Client`from a future that resolves to a`Client`.

[20](https://docs.rs#20)
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! An implementation of the [Cap'n Proto remote procedure call](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html)
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! protocol. Includes all [Level 1](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#protocol-features) features.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! # Example
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! ```capnp
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! # Cap'n Proto schema
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! interface Foo {
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!     identity @0 (x: UInt32) -> (y: UInt32);
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! }
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! ```
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! ```ignore
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! // Rust server defining an implementation of Foo.
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! struct FooImpl;
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! impl foo::Server for FooImpl {
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!     async fn identity(
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!         self: Rc<Self>,
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!         params: foo::IdentityParams,
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!         mut results: foo::IdentityResults
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!     ) -> Result<(), ::capnp::Error> {
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!         let x = params.get()?.get_x();
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!         results.get().set_y(x);
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!         Ok(())
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!     }
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! }
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! ```
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! ```ignore
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! // Rust client calling a remote implementation of Foo.
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! let mut request = foo_client.identity_request();
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! request.get().set_x(123);
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! let promise = request.send().promise.and_then(|response| {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!     println!("results = {}", response.get()?.get_y());
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!     Ok(())
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! });
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! ```
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! For a more complete example, see <https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto-rust/tree/master/capnp-rpc/examples/calculator>
[60](https://docs.rs#60)

[83](https://docs.rs#83)
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// Like [`try!()`], but for functions that return a [`Promise<T, E>`] rather than a [`Result<T, E>`].
[85](https://docs.rs#85)///
[86](https://docs.rs#86)/// Unwraps a `Result<T, E>`. In the case of an error `Err(e)`, immediately returns from the
[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// enclosing function with `Promise::err(e)`.
[88](https://docs.rs#88)#[macro_export]
[89](https://docs.rs#89)macro_rules! pry {
[90](https://docs.rs#90)    ($expr:expr) => {
[91](https://docs.rs#91)        match $expr {
[92](https://docs.rs#92)            ::std::result::Result::Ok(val) => val,
[93](https://docs.rs#93)            ::std::result::Result::Err(err) => {
[94](https://docs.rs#94)                return ::capnp::capability::Promise::err(::std::convert::From::from(err))
[95](https://docs.rs#95)            }
[96](https://docs.rs#96)        }
[97](https://docs.rs#97)    };
[98](https://docs.rs#98)}
[99](https://docs.rs#99)

[102](https://docs.rs#102)mod flow_control;
