[111](https://docs.rs#111)
[112](https://docs.rs#112)use capnp::message;
[113](https://docs.rs#113)
[114](https://docs.rs#114)/// A message to be sent by a [`VatNetwork`].
[115](https://docs.rs#115)pub trait OutgoingMessage {
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    /// Gets the message body, which the caller may fill in any way it wants.
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    ///
[118](https://docs.rs#118)    /// The standard RPC implementation initializes it as a Message as defined
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    /// in `schema/rpc.capnp`.
[120](https://docs.rs#120)    fn get_body(&mut self) -> ::capnp::Result<::capnp::any_pointer::Builder<'_>>;
[121](https://docs.rs#121)
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    /// Same as `get_body()`, but returns the corresponding reader type.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    fn get_body_as_reader(&self) -> ::capnp::Result<::capnp::any_pointer::Reader<'_>>;
[124](https://docs.rs#124)
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// Sends the message. Returns a promise that resolves once the send has completed.
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    /// Dropping the returned promise does *not* cancel the send.
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    fn send(
[128](https://docs.rs#128)        self: Box<Self>,
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    ) -> (
[130](https://docs.rs#130)        Promise<(), Error>,
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        Rc<message::Builder<message::HeapAllocator>>,
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    );
[133](https://docs.rs#133)
[134](https://docs.rs#134)    /// Takes the inner message out of `self`.
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    fn take(self: Box<Self>) -> ::capnp::message::Builder<::capnp::message::HeapAllocator>;
[136](https://docs.rs#136)
[137](https://docs.rs#137)    /// Gets the total size of the message, for flow control purposes. Although the caller
[138](https://docs.rs#138)    /// could also call get_body().target_size(), doing that would walk the message tree,
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    /// whereas typical implementations can compute the size more cheaply by summing
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    /// segment sizes.
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    fn size_in_words(&self) -> usize;
[142](https://docs.rs#142)}
[143](https://docs.rs#143)
[144](https://docs.rs#144)/// A message received from a [`VatNetwork`].
[145](https://docs.rs#145)pub trait IncomingMessage {
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    /// Gets the message body, to be interpreted by the caller.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    ///
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    /// The standard RPC implementation interprets it as a Message as defined
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    /// in `schema/rpc.capnp`.
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    fn get_body(&self) -> ::capnp::Result<::capnp::any_pointer::Reader<'_>>;
[151](https://docs.rs#151)}
[152](https://docs.rs#152)
[153](https://docs.rs#153)/// A two-way RPC connection.
[154](https://docs.rs#154)///
[155](https://docs.rs#155)/// A connection can be created by [`VatNetwork::connect()`].
[156](https://docs.rs#156)pub trait Connection<VatId> {
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    /// Returns the connected vat's authenticated VatId.  It is the VatNetwork's
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    /// responsibility to authenticate this, so that the caller can be assured
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    /// that they are really talking to the identified vat and not an imposter.
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    fn get_peer_vat_id(&self) -> VatId;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    /// Allocates a new message to be sent on this connection.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    ///
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    /// If `first_segment_word_size` is non-zero, it should be treated as a
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    /// hint suggesting how large to make the first segment.  This is entirely
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    /// a hint and the connection may adjust it up or down.  If it is zero,
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    /// the connection should choose the size itself.
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    fn new_outgoing_message(&mut self, first_segment_word_size: u32) -> Box<dyn OutgoingMessage>;
[169](https://docs.rs#169)
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    /// Waits for a message to be received and returns it.  If the read stream cleanly terminates,
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    /// returns None. If any other problem occurs, returns an Error.
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    fn receive_incoming_message(&mut self) -> Promise<Option<Box<dyn IncomingMessage>>, Error>;
[173](https://docs.rs#173)
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    /// Constructs a flow controller for a new stream on this connection.
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    ///
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// Returns (fc, p), where fc is the new flow controller and p is a promise
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    /// that must be polled in order to drive the flow controller.
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    fn new_stream(&mut self) -> (Box<dyn FlowController>, Promise<(), Error>) {
[179](https://docs.rs#179)        let (fc, f) = crate::flow_control::FixedWindowFlowController::new(
[180](https://docs.rs#180)            crate::flow_control::DEFAULT_WINDOW_SIZE,
[181](https://docs.rs#181)        );
[182](https://docs.rs#182)        (Box::new(fc), f)
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    }
[184](https://docs.rs#184)
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    /// Waits until all outgoing messages have been sent, then shuts down the outgoing stream. The
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    /// returned promise resolves after shutdown is complete.
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    fn shutdown(&mut self, result: ::capnp::Result<()>) -> Promise<(), Error>;
[188](https://docs.rs#188)}
[189](https://docs.rs#189)
[190](https://docs.rs#190)/// Tracks a particular RPC stream in order to implement a flow control algorithm.
[191](https://docs.rs#191)pub trait FlowController {
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    fn send(
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        &mut self,
[194](https://docs.rs#194)        message: Box<dyn OutgoingMessage>,
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        ack: Promise<(), Error>,
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    ) -> Promise<(), Error>;
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    fn wait_all_acked(&mut self) -> Promise<(), Error>;
[198](https://docs.rs#198)}
[199](https://docs.rs#199)
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// Network facility between vats, it determines how to form connections between
[201](https://docs.rs#201)/// vats.
[202](https://docs.rs#202)///
[203](https://docs.rs#203)/// ## Vat
[204](https://docs.rs#204)///
[205](https://docs.rs#205)/// Cap'n Proto RPC operates between vats, where a "vat" is some sort of host of
[206](https://docs.rs#206)/// objects.  Typically one Cap'n Proto process (in the Unix sense) is one vat.
[207](https://docs.rs#207)pub trait VatNetwork<VatId> {
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    /// Connects to `host_id`.
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    ///
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    /// Returns None if `host_id` refers to the local vat.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    fn connect(&mut self, host_id: VatId) -> Option<Box<dyn Connection<VatId>>>;
[212](https://docs.rs#212)
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    /// Waits for the next incoming connection and return it.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    fn accept(&mut self) -> Promise<Box<dyn Connection<VatId>>, ::capnp::Error>;
[215](https://docs.rs#215)
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    /// A promise that cannot be resolved until the shutdown.
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    fn drive_until_shutdown(&mut self) -> Promise<(), Error>;
[218](https://docs.rs#218)}
[219](https://docs.rs#219)
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// A portal to objects available on the network.
[221](https://docs.rs#221)///
[222](https://docs.rs#222)/// The RPC implementation sits on top of an implementation of [`VatNetwork`], which
[223](https://docs.rs#223)/// determines how to form connections between vats. The RPC implementation determines
[224](https://docs.rs#224)/// how to use such connections to manage object references and make method calls.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)///
[226](https://docs.rs#226)/// At the moment, this is all rather more general than it needs to be, because the only
[227](https://docs.rs#227)/// implementation of `VatNetwork` is [`twoparty::VatNetwork`]. However, eventually we
[228](https://docs.rs#228)/// will need to have more sophisticated `VatNetwork` implementations, in order to support
[229](https://docs.rs#229)/// [level 3](https://capnproto.org/rpc.html#protocol-features) features.
[230](https://docs.rs#230)///
[231](https://docs.rs#231)/// An `RpcSystem` is a non-`Send`able `Future` and needs to be driven by a task
[232](https://docs.rs#232)/// executor. A common way accomplish that is to pass the `RpcSystem` to
[233](https://docs.rs#233)/// `tokio::task::spawn_local()`.
[234](https://docs.rs#234)#[must_use = "futures do nothing unless polled"]
[235](https://docs.rs#235)pub struct RpcSystem<VatId>
[236](https://docs.rs#236)where
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    VatId: 'static,
[238](https://docs.rs#238){
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    network: Box<dyn crate::VatNetwork<VatId>>,
[240](https://docs.rs#240)
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    bootstrap_cap: Box<dyn ClientHook>,
[242](https://docs.rs#242)
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    // XXX To handle three or more party networks, this should be a map from connection pointers
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    // to connection states.
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    connection_state: Rc<RefCell<Option<Rc<rpc::ConnectionState<VatId>>>>>,
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    tasks: TaskSet<Error>,
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    handle: crate::task_set::TaskSetHandle<Error>,
[249](https://docs.rs#249)}
[250](https://docs.rs#250)
[251](https://docs.rs#251)impl<VatId> RpcSystem<VatId> {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    /// Constructs a new `RpcSystem` with the given network and bootstrap capability.
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    pub fn new(
[254](https://docs.rs#254)        mut network: Box<dyn crate::VatNetwork<VatId>>,
[255](https://docs.rs#255)        bootstrap: Option<::capnp::capability::Client>,
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    ) -> Self {
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        let bootstrap_cap = match bootstrap {
[258](https://docs.rs#258)            Some(cap) => cap.hook,
[259](https://docs.rs#259)            None => broken::new_cap(Error::failed("no bootstrap capability".to_string())),
[260](https://docs.rs#260)        };
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        let (mut handle, tasks) = TaskSet::new(Box::new(SystemTaskReaper));
[262](https://docs.rs#262)
[263](https://docs.rs#263)        let mut handle1 = handle.clone();
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        handle.add(network.drive_until_shutdown().then(move |r| {
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            let r = match r {
[266](https://docs.rs#266)                Ok(()) => Ok(()),
[267](https://docs.rs#267)                Err(e) => {
[268](https://docs.rs#268)                    if e.kind != ::capnp::ErrorKind::Disconnected {
[269](https://docs.rs#269)                        // Don't report disconnects as an error.
[270](https://docs.rs#270)                        Err(e)
[271](https://docs.rs#271)                    } else {
[272](https://docs.rs#272)                        Ok(())
[273](https://docs.rs#273)                    }
[274](https://docs.rs#274)                }
[275](https://docs.rs#275)            };
[276](https://docs.rs#276)
[277](https://docs.rs#277)            handle1.terminate(r);
[278](https://docs.rs#278)            Promise::ok(())
[279](https://docs.rs#279)        }));
[280](https://docs.rs#280)
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        let mut result = Self {
[282](https://docs.rs#282)            network,
[283](https://docs.rs#283)            bootstrap_cap,
[284](https://docs.rs#284)            connection_state: Rc::new(RefCell::new(None)),
[285](https://docs.rs#285)
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            tasks,
[287](https://docs.rs#287)            handle: handle.clone(),
[288](https://docs.rs#288)        };
[289](https://docs.rs#289)
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        let accept_loop = result.accept_loop();
[291](https://docs.rs#291)        handle.add(accept_loop);
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        result
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    }
[294](https://docs.rs#294)
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    /// Connects to the given vat and returns its bootstrap interface, returns
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    /// a client that can be used to invoke the bootstrap interface.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    pub fn bootstrap<T>(&mut self, vat_id: VatId) -> T
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    where
[299](https://docs.rs#299)        T: ::capnp::capability::FromClientHook,
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    {
[301](https://docs.rs#301)        let Some(connection) = self.network.connect(vat_id) else {
[302](https://docs.rs#302)            return T::new(self.bootstrap_cap.clone());
[303](https://docs.rs#303)        };
[304](https://docs.rs#304)        let connection_state = Self::get_connection_state(
[305](https://docs.rs#305)            &self.connection_state,
[306](https://docs.rs#306)            self.bootstrap_cap.clone(),
[307](https://docs.rs#307)            connection,
[308](https://docs.rs#308)            self.handle.clone(),
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        );
[310](https://docs.rs#310)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)        let hook = rpc::ConnectionState::bootstrap(&connection_state);
[312](https://docs.rs#312)        T::new(hook)
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    }
[314](https://docs.rs#314)
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    // not really a loop, because it doesn't need to be for the two party case
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    fn accept_loop(&mut self) -> Promise<(), Error> {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        let connection_state_ref = self.connection_state.clone();
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        let bootstrap_cap = self.bootstrap_cap.clone();
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        let handle = self.handle.clone();
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        Promise::from_future(self.network.accept().map_ok(move |connection| {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)            Self::get_connection_state(&connection_state_ref, bootstrap_cap, connection, handle);
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        }))
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    }
[324](https://docs.rs#324)
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    // If `connection_state_ref` is not already populated, populates it with a new
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    // `ConnectionState` built from a local bootstrap capability and `connection`,
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    // spawning any background tasks onto `handle`. Returns the resulting value
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    // held in `connection_state_ref`.
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    fn get_connection_state(
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        connection_state_ref: &Rc<RefCell<Option<Rc<rpc::ConnectionState<VatId>>>>>,
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        bootstrap_cap: Box<dyn ClientHook>,
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        connection: Box<dyn crate::Connection<VatId>>,
[333](https://docs.rs#333)        mut handle: crate::task_set::TaskSetHandle<Error>,
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    ) -> Rc<rpc::ConnectionState<VatId>> {
[335](https://docs.rs#335)        // TODO this needs to be updated once we allow more general VatNetworks.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        let (tasks, result) = match *connection_state_ref.borrow() {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)            Some(ref connection_state) => {
[338](https://docs.rs#338)                // return early.
[339](https://docs.rs#339)                return connection_state.clone();
[340](https://docs.rs#340)            }
[341](https://docs.rs#341)            None => {
[342](https://docs.rs#342)                let (on_disconnect_fulfiller, on_disconnect_promise) =
[343](https://docs.rs#343)                    oneshot::channel::<Promise<(), Error>>();
[344](https://docs.rs#344)                let connection_state_ref1 = connection_state_ref.clone();
[345](https://docs.rs#345)                handle.add(on_disconnect_promise.then(move |shutdown_promise| {
[346](https://docs.rs#346)                    *connection_state_ref1.borrow_mut() = None;
[347](https://docs.rs#347)                    match shutdown_promise {
[348](https://docs.rs#348)                        Ok(s) => s,
[349](https://docs.rs#349)                        Err(e) => Promise::err(Error::failed(format!("{e}"))),
[350](https://docs.rs#350)                    }
[351](https://docs.rs#351)                }));
[352](https://docs.rs#352)                rpc::ConnectionState::new(bootstrap_cap, connection, on_disconnect_fulfiller)
[353](https://docs.rs#353)            }
[354](https://docs.rs#354)        };
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        *connection_state_ref.borrow_mut() = Some(result.clone());
[356](https://docs.rs#356)        handle.add(tasks);
[357](https://docs.rs#357)        result
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    }
[359](https://docs.rs#359)
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    /// Returns a `Disconnector` future that can be run to cleanly close the connection to this `RpcSystem`'s network.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    /// You should get the `Disconnector` before you spawn the `RpcSystem`.
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    pub fn get_disconnector(&self) -> rpc::Disconnector<VatId> {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)        rpc::Disconnector::new(self.connection_state.clone())
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    }
[365](https://docs.rs#365)}
[366](https://docs.rs#366)
[367](https://docs.rs#367)impl<VatId> Future for RpcSystem<VatId>
[368](https://docs.rs#368)where
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    VatId: 'static,
[370](https://docs.rs#370){
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    type Output = Result<(), Error>;
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context) -> Poll<Self::Output> {
[373](https://docs.rs#373)        Pin::new(&mut self.tasks).poll(cx)
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    }
[375](https://docs.rs#375)}
[376](https://docs.rs#376)
[377](https://docs.rs#377)/// Creates a new local RPC client of type `C` out of an object that implements a server trait `S`.

[379](https://docs.rs#379)where

[381](https://docs.rs#381){

[383](https://docs.rs#383)}
[384](https://docs.rs#384)
[385](https://docs.rs#385)/// Variant of `new_client` that works on an `Rc<S>`.
[386](https://docs.rs#386)pub fn new_client_from_rc<C, S>(s: Rc<S>) -> C
[387](https://docs.rs#387)where
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    C: capnp::capability::FromServer<S>,
[389](https://docs.rs#389){
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    capnp::capability::FromClientHook::new(Box::new(local::Client::new(
[391](https://docs.rs#391)        <C as capnp::capability::FromServer<S>>::from_server(s),
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    )))
[393](https://docs.rs#393)}
[394](https://docs.rs#394)
[395](https://docs.rs#395)/// Collection of unwrappable capabilities.
[396](https://docs.rs#396)///
[397](https://docs.rs#397)/// Allows a server to recognize its own capabilities when passed back to it, and obtain the
[398](https://docs.rs#398)/// underlying Server objects associated with them. Holds only weak references to Server objects
[399](https://docs.rs#399)/// allowing Server objects to be dropped when dropped by the remote client. Call the `gc` method
[400](https://docs.rs#400)/// to reclaim memory used for Server objects that have been dropped.
[401](https://docs.rs#401)pub struct CapabilityServerSet<S, C>
[402](https://docs.rs#402)where
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    C: capnp::capability::FromServer<S>,
[404](https://docs.rs#404){
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    caps: std::collections::HashMap<usize, Weak<S>>,
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    marker: std::marker::PhantomData<C>,
[407](https://docs.rs#407)}
[408](https://docs.rs#408)
[409](https://docs.rs#409)impl<S, C> Default for CapabilityServerSet<S, C>
[410](https://docs.rs#410)where
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    C: capnp::capability::FromServer<S>,
[412](https://docs.rs#412){
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    fn default() -> Self {
[414](https://docs.rs#414)        Self {
[415](https://docs.rs#415)            caps: std::default::Default::default(),
[416](https://docs.rs#416)            marker: std::marker::PhantomData,
[417](https://docs.rs#417)        }
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    }
[419](https://docs.rs#419)}
[420](https://docs.rs#420)
[421](https://docs.rs#421)impl<S, C> CapabilityServerSet<S, C>
[422](https://docs.rs#422)where
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    C: capnp::capability::FromServer<S>,
[424](https://docs.rs#424){
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    pub fn new() -> Self {
[426](https://docs.rs#426)        Self::default()
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    }
[428](https://docs.rs#428)
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    /// Adds a new capability to the set and returns a client backed by it.
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    pub fn new_client(&mut self, s: S) -> C {
[431](https://docs.rs#431)        self.new_client_from_rc(Rc::new(s))
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    }
[433](https://docs.rs#433)
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    /// Variant of `new_client` that works on an `Rc<S>`.
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    pub fn new_client_from_rc(&mut self, rc: Rc<S>) -> C {
[436](https://docs.rs#436)        let weak = Rc::downgrade(&rc);
[437](https://docs.rs#437)        let ptr = Rc::as_ptr(&rc) as usize;
[438](https://docs.rs#438)        self.caps.insert(ptr, weak);
[439](https://docs.rs#439)
[440](https://docs.rs#440)        let dispatch = <C as capnp::capability::FromServer<S>>::from_server(rc);
[441](https://docs.rs#441)        capnp::capability::FromClientHook::new(Box::new(local::Client::new(dispatch)))
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    }
[443](https://docs.rs#443)
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    /// Looks up a capability and returns its underlying server object, if found.
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    /// Fully resolves the capability before looking it up.
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    pub async fn get_local_server(&self, client: &C) -> Option<Rc<S>>
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    where
[448](https://docs.rs#448)        C: capnp::capability::FromClientHook,
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    {
[450](https://docs.rs#450)        let resolved: C = capnp::capability::get_resolved_cap(
[451](https://docs.rs#451)            capnp::capability::FromClientHook::new(client.as_client_hook().add_ref()),
[452](https://docs.rs#452)        )
[453](https://docs.rs#453)        .await;
[454](https://docs.rs#454)        let hook = resolved.into_client_hook();
[455](https://docs.rs#455)        let ptr = hook.get_ptr();
[456](https://docs.rs#456)        self.caps.get(&ptr).and_then(|c| c.upgrade())
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    }
[458](https://docs.rs#458)
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    /// Looks up a capability and returns its underlying server object, if found.
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    /// Does *not* attempt to resolve the capability first, so you will usually want
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    /// to call `get_resolved_cap()` before calling this. The advantage of this method
[462](https://docs.rs#462)    /// over `get_local_server()` is that this one is synchronous and borrows `self`
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    /// over a shorter span (which can be very important if `self` is inside a `RefCell`).
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    pub fn get_local_server_of_resolved(&self, client: &C) -> Option<Rc<S>>
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    where
[466](https://docs.rs#466)        C: capnp::capability::FromClientHook,
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    {
[468](https://docs.rs#468)        let hook = client.as_client_hook();
[469](https://docs.rs#469)        let ptr = hook.get_ptr();
[470](https://docs.rs#470)        self.caps.get(&ptr).and_then(|c| c.upgrade())
[471](https://docs.rs#471)    }
[472](https://docs.rs#472)
[473](https://docs.rs#473)    /// Reclaim memory used for Server objects that no longer exist.
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    pub fn gc(&mut self) {
[475](https://docs.rs#475)        self.caps.retain(|_, c| c.strong_count() > 0);
[476](https://docs.rs#476)    }
[477](https://docs.rs#477)}
[478](https://docs.rs#478)
[479](https://docs.rs#479)/// Creates a `Client` from a future that resolves to a `Client`.
[480](https://docs.rs#480)///
[481](https://docs.rs#481)/// Any calls that arrive before the resolution are accumulated in a queue.
[482](https://docs.rs#482)pub fn new_future_client<T>(
[483](https://docs.rs#483)    client_future: impl ::futures::Future<Output = Result<T, Error>> + 'static,
[484](https://docs.rs#484)) -> T
[485](https://docs.rs#485)where
[486](https://docs.rs#486)    T: ::capnp::capability::FromClientHook,
[487](https://docs.rs#487){
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    let mut queued_client = crate::queued::Client::new(None);
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    let weak_client = Rc::downgrade(&queued_client.inner);
[490](https://docs.rs#490)
[491](https://docs.rs#491)    queued_client.drive(client_future.then(move |r| {
[492](https://docs.rs#492)        if let Some(queued_inner) = weak_client.upgrade() {
[493](https://docs.rs#493)            crate::queued::ClientInner::resolve(&queued_inner, r.map(|c| c.into_client_hook()));
[494](https://docs.rs#494)        }
[495](https://docs.rs#495)        Promise::ok(())
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    }));
[497](https://docs.rs#497)
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    T::new(Box::new(queued_client))
[499](https://docs.rs#499)}
[500](https://docs.rs#500)
[501](https://docs.rs#501)struct SystemTaskReaper;
[502](https://docs.rs#502)impl crate::task_set::TaskReaper<Error> for SystemTaskReaper {
[503](https://docs.rs#503)    fn task_failed(&mut self, error: Error) {
[504](https://docs.rs#504)        println!("ERROR: {error}");
[505](https://docs.rs#505)    }
[506](https://docs.rs#506)}
[507](https://docs.rs#507)
[508](https://docs.rs#508)pub struct ImbuedMessageBuilder<A>
[509](https://docs.rs#509)where
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    A: ::capnp::message::Allocator,
[511](https://docs.rs#511){
[512](https://docs.rs#512)    builder: ::capnp::message::Builder<A>,
[513](https://docs.rs#513)    cap_table: Vec<Option<Box<dyn ::capnp::private::capability::ClientHook>>>,
[514](https://docs.rs#514)}
[515](https://docs.rs#515)

}## Expand description

Network facility between vats, it determines how to form connections between vats.

[§](https://docs.rs#vat)Vat

Cap’n Proto RPC operates between vats, where a “vat” is some sort of host of objects. Typically one Cap’n Proto process (in the Unix sense) is one vat.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Connects to `host_id`.

Returns None if `host_id` refers to the local vat.

# pry in capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/capnp_rpc/macro.pry.html

```
macro_rules! pry {
    ($expr:expr) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Like [ try!()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.try.html), but for functions that return a

[rather than a](https://docs.rs/capnp/0.26.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capnp/capability/struct.Promise.html)

`Promise<T, E>`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result<T, E>`Unwraps a `Result<T, E>`. In the case of an error `Err(e)`, immediately returns from the
enclosing function with `Promise::err(e)`.

# CapabilityServerSet in capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/capnp_rpc/struct.CapabilityServerSet.html

`pub struct CapabilityServerSet<S, C>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Collection of unwrappable capabilities.

Allows a server to recognize its own capabilities when passed back to it, and obtain the
underlying Server objects associated with them. Holds only weak references to Server objects
allowing Server objects to be dropped when dropped by the remote client. Call the `gc` method
to reclaim memory used for Server objects that have been dropped.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/capnp_rpc/lib.rs.html#464-471)#### pub fn [get_local_server_of_resolved](https://docs.rs#method.get_local_server_of_resolved)(&self, client: [&C](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Rc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/rc/struct.Rc.html)<S>>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/capnp_rpc/lib.rs.html#464-471)

#### pub fn [get_local_server_of_resolved](https://docs.rs#method.get_local_server_of_resolved)(&self, client: [&C](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Rc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/rc/struct.Rc.html)<S>>

Looks up a capability and returns its underlying server object, if found.
Does *not* attempt to resolve the capability first, so you will usually want
to call `get_resolved_cap()` before calling this. The advantage of this method
over `get_local_server()` is that this one is synchronous and borrows `self`
over a shorter span (which can be very important if `self` is inside a `RefCell`).

{  }Expand description A portal to objects available on the network.

The RPC implementation sits on top of an implementation of `VatNetwork`

At the moment, this is all rather more general than it needs to be, because the only
implementation of `VatNetwork` is `twoparty::VatNetwork``VatNetwork` implementations, in order to support
level 3  features.

An `RpcSystem` is a non-`Send`able `Future` and needs to be driven by a task
executor. A common way accomplish that is to pass the `RpcSystem` to
`tokio::task::spawn_local()`.

Constructs a new `RpcSystem` with the given network and bootstrap capability.

Connects to the given vat and returns its bootstrap interface, returns
a client that can be used to invoke the bootstrap interface.

Returns a `Disconnector` future that can be run to cleanly close the connection to this `RpcSystem`’s network.
You should get the `Disconnector` before you spawn the `RpcSystem`.

If `first_segment_word_size` is non-zero, it should be treated as a
hint suggesting how large to make the first segment.  This is entirely
a hint and the connection may adjust it up or down.  If it is zero,
the connection should choose the size itself.

# SetTarget in capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/capnp_rpc/trait.SetTarget.html

pub trait SetTarget<C> {
    // Required methods
    fn
```
[add_ref](https://docs.rs#tymethod.add_ref)(&self) -> [Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [SetTarget](https://docs.rs/trait.SetTarget.html)<C>>;
[set_target](https://docs.rs#tymethod.set_target)(&self, target: C);
}## Expand description

Trait implemented by the reconnecting client to set new connection out-of-band.

When using [ auto_reconnect](https://docs.rs/fn.auto_reconnect.html) or

[it is not always optimal to wait for a call to fail with](https://docs.rs/fn.lazy_auto_reconnect.html)

`lazy_auto_reconnect`[before replacing the client that is wrapped with a new fresh one.](https://docs.rs/capnp/0.26.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capnp/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.Disconnected)

`Disconnected`Sometimes we know by other means that a client has gone away. It could be that we have clients that automatically sends us a new capability when it reconnects to us.

For these situations you can use the implementation of this trait that you get from
[ auto_reconnect](https://docs.rs/fn.auto_reconnect.html) or

[to manually set the target of the wrapped client.](https://docs.rs/fn.lazy_auto_reconnect.html)

`lazy_auto_reconnect`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// The reconnecting client that automatically calls connect
let (foo_client, set_target) = auto_reconnect(|| {
    Ok(new_future_client(connect()))
})?;
// do work with foo_client
...
// We become aware that the client has gone so reconnect manually
set_target.set_target(new_future_client(connect()));
// do more work with foo_client
...
```

# auto_reconnect in capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/capnp_rpc/fn.auto_reconnect.html

## Expand description

Creates a new client that reconnects when getting [ ErrorKind::Disconnected](https://docs.rs/capnp/0.26.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capnp/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.Disconnected) errors.

Usually when you get a [ Disconnected](https://docs.rs/capnp/0.26.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capnp/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.Disconnected) error response from calling a method on a capability
it means the end of that capability for good. And so you can’t call methods on that
capability any more.

When you have a way of getting the capability back: Be it from a bootstrap or because
the capability is persistent this method can help you wrap that reconnection logic into a client
that automatically runs the logic whenever a method call returns [ Disconnected](https://docs.rs/capnp/0.26.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capnp/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.Disconnected).

The way it works is that you provide a closure that returns a fresh client or a permanent error and
you get a new connected client and a [ SetTarget](https://docs.rs/trait.SetTarget.html) interface that you can optionally use to prematurely
replace the client.

There is one caveat though: The original request that got a [ Disconnected](https://docs.rs/capnp/0.26.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capnp/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.Disconnected)
will still get that response. It is up to the caller to retry the call if relevant. `auto_reconnect`` only
deals with the calls that come after.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
# Cap'n Proto schema
interface Foo {
    identity @0 (x: UInt32) -> (y: UInt32);
}
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// A simple bootstrapped tcp connection to remote.example.com
async fn connect() -> capnp::Result<foo_client::Client> {
    let stream = tokio::net::TcpStream::connect(&"remote.example.com:3001").await?;
    stream.set_nodelay(true)?;
    let (reader, writer) = tokio_util::compat::TokioAsyncReadCompatExt::compat(stream).split();
    let network = Box::new(twoparty::VatNetwork::new(
        futures::io::BufReader::new(reader),
        futures::io::BufWriter::new(writer),
        rpc_twoparty_capnp::Side::Client,
        Default::default(),
    ));
    let mut rpc_system = RpcSystem::new(network, None);
    let foo_client: foo_client::Client = rpc_system.bootstrap(rpc_twoparty_capnp::Side::Server);
    tokio::task::spawn_local(rpc_system);
    Ok(foo_client)
}
// The reconnecting client that automatically calls connect
let (foo_client, _) = auto_reconnect(|| {
    // By using new_future_client we delay any calls until we have a new connection.
    Ok(new_future_client(connect()))
})?;
// Calling Foo like normally.
let mut request = foo_client.identity_request();
request.get().set_x(123);
let promise = request.send().promise.and_then(|response| {
    println!("results = {}", response.get()?.get_y());
    Ok(())
});
```

---

# lazy_auto_reconnect in capnp_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp-rpc/0.26.1/capnp_rpc/fn.lazy_auto_reconnect.html

## Expand description

Creates a new client that lazily connect and also reconnects when getting [ ErrorKind::Disconnected](https://docs.rs/capnp/0.26.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capnp/enum.ErrorKind.html#variant.Disconnected) errors.

For explanation of how this functions see: `auto_reconnect`

The main difference between [ auto_reconnect](https://docs.rs/fn.auto_reconnect.html) and this function is that while

[will call the closure immediately to get an inner client to wrap, this function starts out disconnected and only calls the closure to get the actual client when the capability is first used.](https://docs.rs/fn.auto_reconnect.html)

`auto_reconnect`

# embedded_io - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/embedded-io/^0.7.1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#embedded-io)`embedded-io`

This project is developed and maintained by the [HAL team](https://github.com/rust-embedded/wg#the-hal-team).

Input/Output traits for embedded systems.

Rust’s `std::io` traits are not available in `no_std` targets, mainly because `std::io::Error`
requires allocation. This crate contains replacement equivalent traits, usable in `no_std`
targets.

[§](https://docs.rs#differences-with-stdio)Differences with `std::io`

- `Error`is an associated type. This allows each implementor to return its own error type, while avoiding- `dyn`or- `Box`. This is consistent with how errors are handled in- `embedded-hal`
- In `std::io`, the`Read`/`Write`traits might be blocking or non-blocking (i.e. returning`WouldBlock`errors) depending on the file descriptor’s mode, which is only known at run-time. This allows passing a non-blocking stream to code that expects a blocking stream, causing unexpected errors. To solve this,`embedded-io`specifies`Read`/`Write`are always blocking, and adds new`ReadReady`/`WriteReady`traits to allow using streams in a non-blocking way.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-cargo-features)Optional Cargo features

- `std`- `From`impls to convert to/from- `std::io`structs.
- `alloc`- `Box`, adds- `Write`impl to- `Vec`.
- `defmt`- `defmt::Format`from- `defmt`1.x for enums and structs.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version-msrv)Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate is guaranteed to compile on stable Rust 1.81 and up. It *might*
compile with older versions but that may change in any new patch release.

See [here](https://docs.rs/docs/msrv.md) for details on how the MSRV may be upgraded.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

[§](https://docs.rs#contribution)Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorKind.html)- Kind
- Possible kinds of errors.
- [Read](https://docs.rs/enum.ReadExactError.html)- Exact - Error
- Error returned by `Read::read_exact`
- [Seek](https://docs.rs/enum.SeekFrom.html)- From
- Enumeration of possible methods to seek within an I/O object.
- [Slice](https://docs.rs/enum.SliceWriteError.html)- Write - Error
- Errors that could be returned by `Write`on`&mut [u8]`.
- [Write](https://docs.rs/enum.WriteFmtError.html)- FmtError
- Error returned by `Write::write_fmt`

# quickcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quickcheck/^1/

## Expand description

This crate is a port of
[Haskell’s QuickCheck](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/QuickCheck).

QuickCheck is a library for random testing of program properties. The programmer provides a specification of the program, in the form of properties which functions should satisfy, and QuickCheck then tests that the properties hold in a large number of randomly generated cases.

For detailed examples, please see the
[README](https://github.com/BurntSushi/quickcheck).

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

In general, this crate considers the `Arbitrary` implementations provided as
implementation details. Strategies may or may not change over time, which may
cause new test failures, presumably due to the discovery of new bugs due to a
new kind of witness being generated. These sorts of changes may happen in
semver compatible releases.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/macro.quickcheck.html)
- A macro for writing quickcheck tests.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Gen](https://docs.rs/struct.Gen.html)
- `Gen`represents a PRNG.
- [NoShrink](https://docs.rs/struct.NoShrink.html)
- Wrapper for disabling shrinking for an Arbitrary
- [Quick](https://docs.rs/struct.QuickCheck.html)- Check
- The main `QuickCheck`type for setting configuration and running`QuickCheck`.
- [Test](https://docs.rs/struct.TestResult.html)- Result
- Describes the status of a single instance of a test.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- `Arbitrary`describes types whose values can be randomly generated and shrunk.
- [Testable](https://docs.rs/trait.Testable.html)
- `Testable`describes types (e.g., a function) whose values can be tested.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [empty_](https://docs.rs/fn.empty_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with zero elements.
- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/fn.quickcheck.html)
- Convenience function for running `QuickCheck`.
- [single_](https://docs.rs/fn.single_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with a single element.

# capnp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capnp/0.26.1/target-redirect/capnp/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#capn-proto-runtime-library)Cap’n Proto Runtime Library

This crate contains basic facilities for reading and writing
[Cap’n Proto](https://capnproto.org) messages in Rust. It is intended to
be used in conjunction with code generated by the
[capnpc-rust](https://crates.io/crates/capnpc) crate.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [any_](https://docs.rs/any_pointer/index.html)- pointer
- Untyped pointer that can be cast to any struct, list, or capability type.
- [any_](https://docs.rs/any_pointer_list/index.html)- pointer_ - list
- List of AnyPointers.
- [capability](https://docs.rs/capability/index.html)
- Hooks for the RPC system.
- [capability_](https://docs.rs/capability_list/index.html)- list
- List of capabilities.
- [constant](https://docs.rs/constant/index.html)
- Helper type for generated Struct and List constants.
- [data](https://docs.rs/data/index.html)
- Sequence of bytes.
- [data_](https://docs.rs/data_list/index.html)- list
- List of sequences of bytes.
- [dynamic_](https://docs.rs/dynamic_list/index.html)- list
- Dynamically-typed lists.
- [dynamic_](https://docs.rs/dynamic_struct/index.html)- struct
- Dynamically-typed structs.
- [dynamic_](https://docs.rs/dynamic_value/index.html)- value
- Dynamically typed values.
- [enum_](https://docs.rs/enum_list/index.html)- list
- List of enums.
- [introspect](https://docs.rs/introspect/index.html)
- Traits and types to support run-time type introspection, i.e. reflection.
- [io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html)
- Custom I/O traits that roughly mirror `std::io::{Read, BufRead, Write}`. This extra layer of indirection enables support of no-std environments.
- [list_](https://docs.rs/list_list/index.html)- list
- List of lists.
- [message](https://docs.rs/message/index.html)
- Untyped root container for a Cap’n Proto value.
- [primitive_](https://docs.rs/primitive_list/index.html)- list
- List of primitives.
- [private](https://docs.rs/private/index.html)
- Implementation details that should never be directly used by clients.
- [raw](https://docs.rs/raw/index.html)
- Functions providing low level access to encoded data.
- [schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)
- Convenience wrappers of the datatypes defined in schema.capnp.
- [schema_](https://docs.rs/schema_capnp/index.html)- capnp
- Code generated from
[schema.capnp](https://github.com/capnproto/capnproto/blob/master/c%2B%2B/src/capnp/schema.capnp).
- [serialize](https://docs.rs/serialize/index.html)
- Reading and writing of messages using the
[standard stream framing](https://capnproto.org/encoding.html#serialization-over-a-stream).
- [serialize_](https://docs.rs/serialize_packed/index.html)- packed
- Reading and writing of messages using the
[packed stream encoding](https://capnproto.org/encoding.html#packing).
- [struct_](https://docs.rs/struct_list/index.html)- list
- List of structs.
- [text](https://docs.rs/text/index.html)
- UTF-8 encoded text.
- [text_](https://docs.rs/text_list/index.html)- list
- List of strings containing UTF-8 encoded text.
- [traits](https://docs.rs/traits/index.html)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [generated_](https://docs.rs/macro.generated_code.html)- code
- Macro for importing Rust code that has been generated by `capnpc::CompilerCommand`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Describes an arbitrary error that prevented an operation from completing.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.MessageSize.html)- Size
- Size of a message. Every generated struct has a method `.total_size()`that returns this.
- [NotIn](https://docs.rs/struct.NotInSchema.html)- Schema
- An enum value or union discriminant that was not found among those defined in a schema.
- [Word](https://docs.rs/struct.Word.html)
- 8 bytes, aligned to an 8-byte boundary.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorKind.html)- Kind
- The general nature of an error. The purpose of this enum is not to describe the error itself, but rather to describe how the client might want to respond to the error.
- [Output](https://docs.rs/enum.OutputSegments.html)- Segments
- Helper struct that allows `MessageBuilder::get_segments_for_output()`to avoid heap allocations in the single-segment case.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- Constructs a word with the given bytes.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- Because messages are lazily validated, the return type of any method that reads a pointer field must be wrapped in a Result.

# generated_code in capnp - Rust

```
macro_rules! generated_code {
    ($vis:vis mod $mod_name:ident, $file_name:expr) => { ... };
    ($vis:vis mod $mod_name:ident) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Macro for importing Rust code that has been generated by `capnpc::CompilerCommand`.

For example:

pulls in the generated code for `foo.capnp` into a module named `foo_capnp`.
It expects to find the generated code in a file `$OUT_DIR/foo_capnp.rs`,
where `OUT_DIR` is Cargo’s standard environment variable giving the
location of the output of `build.rs`.

If the generated code lives in a nonstandard location—perhaps in a subdirectory
of `OUT_DIR`—you can specify its path as a second argument:

# Word in capnp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp/^0.26.0/struct.Word.html

`pub struct Word { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

8 bytes, aligned to an 8-byte boundary.

Internally, capnproto-rust allocates message buffers using this type, to guarantee alignment.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

    TypeMismatch,
    UnalignedSegment,
    UnexpectedFarPointer,
    UnknownPointerType,
}## Expand description

The general nature of an error. The purpose of this enum is not to describe the error itself, but rather to describe how the client might want to respond to the error.

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Failed)

### Failed

Something went wrong

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Overloaded)

### Overloaded

The call failed because of a temporary lack of resources. This could be space resources (out of memory, out of disk space) or time resources (request queue overflow, operation timed out).

The operation might work if tried again, but it should NOT be repeated immediately as this may simply exacerbate the problem.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Disconnected)

### Disconnected

The call required communication over a connection that has been lost. The caller will need to re-establish connections and try again.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Unimplemented)

### Unimplemented

The requested method is not implemented. The caller may wish to revert to a fallback approach based on other methods.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.BufferNotLargeEnough)

### BufferNotLargeEnough

Buffer is not large enough

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CannotCreateACanonicalMessageWithACapability)

### CannotCreateACanonicalMessageWithACapability

Cannot create a canonical message with a capability

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CannotSetAnyPointerFieldToAPrimitiveValue)

### CannotSetAnyPointerFieldToAPrimitiveValue

Cannot set AnyPointer field to a primitive value

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CantHandleNonStructInlineComposite)

### CantHandleNonStructInlineComposite

Don’t know how to handle non-STRUCT inline composite.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.EmptyBuffer)

### EmptyBuffer

Empty buffer

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.EmptySlice)

### EmptySlice

Empty slice

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.EnumValueOrUnionDiscriminantNotPresent)

### EnumValueOrUnionDiscriminantNotPresent([NotInSchema](https://docs.rs/struct.NotInSchema.html))

Enum value or union discriminant {} was not present in schema

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ExistingListPointerIsNotByteSized)

# OutputSegments in capnp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capnp/^0.26.0/enum.OutputSegments.html

## Expand description

Helper struct that allows `MessageBuilder::get_segments_for_output()` to avoid heap allocations
in the single-segment case.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

1.5.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#198)#### pub fn [split_first](https://docs.rs#method.split_first)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<([&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html), &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html))>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#198)

#### pub fn [split_first](https://docs.rs#method.split_first)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<([&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html), &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html))>

Returns the first and all the rest of the elements of the slice, or `None` if it is empty.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
let x = &[0, 1, 2];
if let Some((first, elements)) = x.split_first() {
    assert_eq!(first, &0);
    assert_eq!(elements, &[1, 2]);
}
```
1.5.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#240)#### pub fn [split_last](https://docs.rs#method.split_last)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<([&T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html), &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html))>

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
let x = &[0, 1, 2];
if let Some((last, elements)) = x.split_last() {
    assert_eq!(last, &2);
    assert_eq!(elements, &[0, 1]);
}
```
1.77.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#327)#### pub fn [first_chunk](https://docs.rs#method.first_chunk)<const N: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<&[[T; N]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#327)

#### pub fn [first_chunk](https://docs.rs#method.first_chunk)<const N: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<&[[T; N]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)>

Returns an array reference to the first `N` items in the slice.

If the slice is not at least `N` in length, this will return `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
let u = [10, 40, 30];
assert_eq!(Some(&[10, 40]), u.first_chunk::<2>());
let v: &[i32] = &[10];
assert_eq!(None, v.first_chunk::<2>());
let w: &[i32] = &[];
assert_eq!(Some(&[]), w.first_chunk::<0>());
```
Returns an array reference to the first `N` items in the slice and the remaining slice.

If the slice is not at least `N` in length, this will return `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
let x = &[0, 1, 2];
if let Some((first, elements)) = x.split_first_chunk::<2>() {
    assert_eq!(first, &[0, 1]);
    assert_eq!(elements, &[2]);
}
assert_eq!(None, x.split_first_chunk::<4>());
```
Returns an array reference to the last `N` items in the slice and the remaining slice.

If the slice is not at least `N` in length, this will return `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
let x = &[0, 1, 2];
if let Some((elements, last)) = x.split_last_chunk::<2>() {
    assert_eq!(elements, &[0]);
    assert_eq!(last, &[1, 2]);
}
assert_eq!(None, x.split_last_chunk::<4>());
```

1.0.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#640-642)#### pub unsafe fn [get_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.get_unchecked)<I>(
    &self,
    index: I,
) -> &<I as [SliceIndex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html)<[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)>>::[Output](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html#associatedtype.Output)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#640-642)

#### pub unsafe fn [get_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.get_unchecked)<I>(
    &self,
    index: I,
) -> &<I as [SliceIndex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html)<[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)>>::[Output](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html#associatedtype.Output)

Returns a reference to an element or subslice, without doing bounds checking.

For a safe alternative see [ get](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.get).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Calling this method with an out-of-bounds index is * undefined behavior*
even if the resulting reference is not used.

You can think of this like `.get(index).unwrap_unchecked()`.  It’s UB
to call `.get_unchecked(len)`, even if you immediately convert to a
pointer.  And it’s UB to call `.get_unchecked(..len + 1)`,
`.get_unchecked(..=len)`, or similar.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
let x = &[1, 2, 4];
unsafe {
    assert_eq!(x.get_unchecked(1), &2);
}
```
Returns a raw pointer to the slice’s buffer.

The caller must ensure that the slice outlives the pointer this function returns, or else it will end up dangling.

The caller must also ensure that the memory the pointer (non-transitively) points to
is never written to (except inside an `UnsafeCell`) using this pointer or any pointer
derived from it. If you need to mutate the contents of the slice, use [ as_mut_ptr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.as_mut_ptr).

Modifying the container referenced by this slice may cause its buffer to be reallocated, which would also make any pointers to it invalid.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
let x = &[1, 2, 4];
let x_ptr = x.as_ptr();
unsafe {
    for i in 0..x.len() {
        assert_eq!(x.get_unchecked(i), &*x_ptr.add(i));
    }
}
```
1.48.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#796)#### pub fn [as_ptr_range](https://docs.rs#method.as_ptr_range)(&self) -> [Range](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/range/struct.Range.html)<[*const T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#796)

#### pub fn [as_ptr_range](https://docs.rs#method.as_ptr_range)(&self) -> [Range](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/range/struct.Range.html)<[*const T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.pointer.html)>

Returns the two raw pointers spanning the slice.

The returned range is half-open, which means that the end pointer
points *one past* the last element of the slice. This way, an empty
slice is represented by two equal pointers, and the difference between
the two pointers represents the size of the slice.

See [ as_ptr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.as_ptr) for warnings on using these pointers. The end pointer
requires extra caution, as it does not point to a valid element in the
slice.

This function is useful for interacting with foreign interfaces which use two pointers to refer to a range of elements in memory, as is common in C++.

It can also be useful to check if a pointer to an element refers to an element of this slice:

```
let a = [1, 2, 3];
let x = &a[1] as *const _;
let y = &5 as *const _;
assert!(a.as_ptr_range().contains(&x));
assert!(!a.as_ptr_range().contains(&y));
```
Gets a reference to the underlying array.

If `N` is not exactly equal to the length of `self`, then this method returns `None`.

Returns an iterator over the slice.

The iterator yields all items from start to end.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
let x = &[1, 2, 4];
let mut iterator = x.iter();
assert_eq!(iterator.next(), Some(&1));
assert_eq!(iterator.next(), Some(&2));
assert_eq!(iterator.next(), Some(&4));
assert_eq!(iterator.next(), None);
```
Returns an iterator over all contiguous windows of length
`size`. The windows overlap. If the slice is shorter than
`size`, the iterator returns no values.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if `size` is zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
let slice = ['l', 'o', 'r', 'e', 'm'];
let mut iter = slice.windows(3);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &['l', 'o', 'r']);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &['o', 'r', 'e']);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &['r', 'e', 'm']);
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
If the slice is shorter than `size`:

```
let slice = ['f', 'o', 'o'];
let mut iter = slice.windows(4);
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
Because the [Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html) trait cannot represent the required lifetimes,
there is no `windows_mut` analog to `windows`;
`[0,1,2].windows_mut(2).collect()` would violate [the rules of references](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-02-references-and-borrowing.html#the-rules-of-references)
(though a [LendingIterator](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2022/10/28/gats-stabilization.html) analog is possible). You can sometimes use
[ Cell::as_slice_of_cells](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cell/struct.Cell.html#method.as_slice_of_cells) in
conjunction with

`windows` instead:```
use std::cell::Cell;
let mut array = ['R', 'u', 's', 't', ' ', '2', '0', '1', '5'];
let slice = &mut array[..];
let slice_of_cells: &[Cell<char>] = Cell::from_mut(slice).as_slice_of_cells();
for w in slice_of_cells.windows(3) {
    Cell::swap(&w[0], &w[2]);
}
assert_eq!(array, ['s', 't', ' ', '2', '0', '1', '5', 'u', 'R']);
```
Returns an iterator over `chunk_size` elements of the slice at a time, starting at the
beginning of the slice.

The chunks are slices and do not overlap. If `chunk_size` does not divide the length of the
slice, then the last chunk will not have length `chunk_size`.

See [ chunks_exact](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.chunks_exact) for a variant of this iterator that returns chunks of always exactly

`chunk_size` elements, and [for the same iterator but starting at the end of the slice.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.rchunks)

`rchunks`If your `chunk_size` is a constant, consider using [ as_chunks](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.as_chunks) instead, which will
give references to arrays of exactly that length, rather than slices.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

Panics if `chunk_size` is zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
let slice = ['l', 'o', 'r', 'e', 'm'];
let mut iter = slice.chunks(2);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &['l', 'o']);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &['r', 'e']);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &['m']);
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
1.31.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#1245)#### pub fn [chunks_exact](https://docs.rs#method.chunks_exact)(&self, chunk_size: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [ChunksExact](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/iter/struct.ChunksExact.html)<'_, T>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#1245)

#### pub fn [chunks_exact](https://docs.rs#method.chunks_exact)(&self, chunk_size: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [ChunksExact](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/iter/struct.ChunksExact.html)<'_, T>

Returns an iterator over `chunk_size` elements of the slice at a time, starting at the
beginning of the slice.

The chunks are slices and do not overlap. If `chunk_size` does not divide the length of the
slice, then the last up to `chunk_size-1` elements will be omitted and can be retrieved
from the `remainder` function of the iterator.

Due to each chunk having exactly `chunk_size` elements, the compiler can often optimize the
resulting code better than in the case of [ chunks](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.chunks).

See [ chunks](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.chunks) for a variant of this iterator that also returns the remainder as a smaller
chunk, and

[for the same iterator but starting at the end of the slice.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.rchunks_exact)

`rchunks_exact`If your `chunk_size` is a constant, consider using [ as_chunks](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.as_chunks) instead, which will
give references to arrays of exactly that length, rather than slices.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-2)Panics

Panics if `chunk_size` is zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

```
let slice = ['l', 'o', 'r', 'e', 'm'];
let mut iter = slice.chunks_exact(2);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &['l', 'o']);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &['r', 'e']);
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
assert_eq!(iter.remainder(), &['m']);
```
1.88.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#1341)#### pub unsafe fn [as_chunks_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.as_chunks_unchecked)<const N: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>(&self) -> &[[[T; N]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)]

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#1341)

#### pub unsafe fn [as_chunks_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.as_chunks_unchecked)<const N: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>(&self) -> &[[[T; N]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)]

Splits the slice into a slice of `N`-element arrays,
assuming that there’s no remainder.

This is the inverse operation to [ as_flattened](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.as_flattened).

As this is `unsafe`, consider whether you could use [ as_chunks](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.as_chunks) or

[instead, perhaps via something like](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.as_rchunks)

`as_rchunks``if let (chunks, []) = slice.as_chunks()` or
`let (chunks, []) = slice.as_chunks() else { unreachable!() };`.[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

This may only be called when

- The slice splits exactly into `N`-element chunks (aka`self.len() % N == 0`).
- `N != 0`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

```
let slice: &[char] = &['l', 'o', 'r', 'e', 'm', '!'];
let chunks: &[[char; 1]] =
    // SAFETY: 1-element chunks never have remainder
    unsafe { slice.as_chunks_unchecked() };
assert_eq!(chunks, &[['l'], ['o'], ['r'], ['e'], ['m'], ['!']]);
let chunks: &[[char; 3]] =
    // SAFETY: The slice length (6) is a multiple of 3
    unsafe { slice.as_chunks_unchecked() };
assert_eq!(chunks, &[['l', 'o', 'r'], ['e', 'm', '!']]);
// These would be unsound:
// let chunks: &[[_; 5]] = slice.as_chunks_unchecked() // The slice length is not a multiple of 5
// let chunks: &[[_; 0]] = slice.as_chunks_unchecked() // Zero-length chunks are never allowed
```
Splits the slice into a slice of `N`-element arrays,
starting at the beginning of the slice,
and a remainder slice with length strictly less than `N`.

The remainder is meaningful in the division sense.  Given
`let (chunks, remainder) = slice.as_chunks()`, then:

- `chunks.len()`equals- `slice.len() / N`,
- `remainder.len()`equals- `slice.len() % N`, and
- `slice.len()`equals- `chunks.len() * N + remainder.len()`.

You can flatten the chunks back into a slice-of-`T` with [ as_flattened](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.as_flattened).

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-3)Panics

Panics if `N` is zero.

Note that this check is against a const generic parameter, not a runtime value, and thus a particular monomorphization will either always panic or it will never panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-18)Examples

```
let slice = ['l', 'o', 'r', 'e', 'm'];
let (chunks, remainder) = slice.as_chunks();
assert_eq!(chunks, &[['l', 'o'], ['r', 'e']]);
assert_eq!(remainder, &['m']);
```
If you expect the slice to be an exact multiple, you can combine
`let`-`else` with an empty slice pattern:

```
let slice = ['R', 'u', 's', 't'];
let (chunks, []) = slice.as_chunks::<2>() else {
    panic!("slice didn't have even length")
};
assert_eq!(chunks, &[['R', 'u'], ['s', 't']]);
```
1.88.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#1446)#### pub fn [as_rchunks](https://docs.rs#method.as_rchunks)<const N: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>(&self) -> (&[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html), &[[[T; N]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)])

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#1446)

#### pub fn [as_rchunks](https://docs.rs#method.as_rchunks)<const N: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>(&self) -> (&[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html), &[[[T; N]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)])

Splits the slice into a slice of `N`-element arrays,
starting at the end of the slice,
and a remainder slice with length strictly less than `N`.

The remainder is meaningful in the division sense.  Given
`let (remainder, chunks) = slice.as_rchunks()`, then:

- `remainder.len()`equals- `slice.len() % N`,
- `chunks.len()`equals- `slice.len() / N`, and
- `slice.len()`equals- `chunks.len() * N + remainder.len()`.

You can flatten the chunks back into a slice-of-`T` with [ as_flattened](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.as_flattened).

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-4)Panics

Panics if `N` is zero.

Note that this check is against a const generic parameter, not a runtime value, and thus a particular monomorphization will either always panic or it will never panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-19)Examples

```
let slice = ['l', 'o', 'r', 'e', 'm'];
let (remainder, chunks) = slice.as_rchunks();
assert_eq!(remainder, &['l']);
assert_eq!(chunks, &[['o', 'r'], ['e', 'm']]);

1.31.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#1778)#### pub fn [rchunks_exact](https://docs.rs#method.rchunks_exact)(&self, chunk_size: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [RChunksExact](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/iter/struct.RChunksExact.html)<'_, T>

Returns an iterator over `chunk_size` elements of the slice at a time, starting at the
end of the slice.

The chunks are slices and do not overlap. If `chunk_size` does not divide the length of the
slice, then the last up to `chunk_size-1` elements will be omitted and can be retrieved
from the `remainder` function of the iterator.

Due to each chunk having exactly `chunk_size` elements, the compiler can often optimize the

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-7)Panics

Panics if `chunk_size` is zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-22)Examples

```
let slice = ['l', 'o', 'r', 'e', 'm'];
let mut iter = slice.rchunks_exact(2);

assert!(iter.next().is_none());

```
Returns an iterator over the slice producing non-overlapping runs of elements using the predicate to separate them.

The predicate is called for every pair of consecutive elements,
meaning that it is called on `slice[0]` and `slice[1]`,
followed by `slice[1]` and `slice[2]`, and so on.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-23)Examples

```
let slice = &[1, 1, 1, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2];
let mut iter = slice.chunk_by(|a, b| a == b);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(&[1, 1, 1][..]));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(&[3, 3][..]));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(&[2, 2, 2][..]));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), None);
```
This method can be used to extract the sorted subslices:

```
let slice = &[1, 1, 2, 3, 2, 3, 2, 3, 4];
let mut iter = slice.chunk_by(|a, b| a <= b);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(&[1, 1, 2, 3][..]));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(&[2, 3][..]));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(&[2, 3, 4][..]));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), None);
```
Divides one slice into two at an index.

The first will contain all indices from `[0, mid)` (excluding
the index `mid` itself) and the second will contain all
indices from `[mid, len)` (excluding the index `len` itself).

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-8)Panics

Panics if `mid > len`.  For a non-panicking alternative see
[ split_at_checked](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.split_at_checked).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-24)Examples

```
let v = ['a', 'b', 'c'];
{
   let (left, right) = v.split_at(0);
   assert_eq!(left, []);
   assert_eq!(right, ['a', 'b', 'c']);
}
{
    let (left, right) = v.split_at(2);
    assert_eq!(left, ['a', 'b']);
    assert_eq!(right, ['c']);
}
{
    let (left, right) = v.split_at(3);
    assert_eq!(left, ['a', 'b', 'c']);
    assert_eq!(right, []);
}
```
1.79.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#2041)#### pub unsafe fn [split_at_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.split_at_unchecked)(&self, mid: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> (&[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html), &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html))

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#2041)

#### pub unsafe fn [split_at_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.split_at_unchecked)(&self, mid: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> (&[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html), &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html))

Divides one slice into two at an index, without doing bounds checking.

The first will contain all indices from `[0, mid)` (excluding
the index `mid` itself) and the second will contain all
indices from `[mid, len)` (excluding the index `len` itself).

For a safe alternative see [ split_at](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.split_at).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-2)Safety

Calling this method with an out-of-bounds index is * undefined behavior*
even if the resulting reference is not used. The caller has to ensure that

`0 <= mid <= self.len()`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-25)Examples

```
let v = ['a', 'b', 'c'];
unsafe {
   let (left, right) = v.split_at_unchecked(0);
   assert_eq!(left, []);
   assert_eq!(right, ['a', 'b', 'c']);
}
unsafe {
    let (left, right) = v.split_at_unchecked(2);
    assert_eq!(left, ['a', 'b']);
    assert_eq!(right, ['c']);
}
unsafe {
    let (left, right) = v.split_at_unchecked(3);
    assert_eq!(left, ['a', 'b', 'c']);
    assert_eq!(right, []);
}
```
Divides one slice into two at an index, returning `None` if the slice is
too short.

If `mid ≤ len` returns a pair of slices where the first will contain all
indices from `[0, mid)` (excluding the index `mid` itself) and the
second will contain all indices from `[mid, len)` (excluding the index
`len` itself).

Otherwise, if `mid > len`, returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-26)Examples

```
let v = [1, -2, 3, -4, 5, -6];
{
   let (left, right) = v.split_at_checked(0).unwrap();
   assert_eq!(left, []);
   assert_eq!(right, [1, -2, 3, -4, 5, -6]);
}
{
    let (left, right) = v.split_at_checked(2).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(left, [1, -2]);
    assert_eq!(right, [3, -4, 5, -6]);
}
{
    let (left, right) = v.split_at_checked(6).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(left, [1, -2, 3, -4, 5, -6]);
    assert_eq!(right, []);
}
assert_eq!(None, v.split_at_checked(7));
```
Returns an iterator over subslices separated by elements that match
`pred`. The matched element is not contained in the subslices.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-27)Examples

```
let slice = [10, 40, 33, 20];
let mut iter = slice.split(|num| num % 3 == 0);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &[10, 40]);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &[20]);
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
If the first element is matched, an empty slice will be the first item returned by the iterator. Similarly, if the last element in the slice is matched, an empty slice will be the last item returned by the iterator:

```
let slice = [10, 40, 33];
let mut iter = slice.split(|num| num % 3 == 0);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &[10, 40]);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &[]);
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
If two matched elements are directly adjacent, an empty slice will be present between them:

```
let slice = [10, 6, 33, 20];
let mut iter = slice.split(|num| num % 3 == 0);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &[10]);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &[]);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &[20]);
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
1.51.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#2305-2307)#### pub fn [split_inclusive](https://docs.rs#method.split_inclusive)<F>(&self, pred: F) -> [SplitInclusive](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/iter/struct.SplitInclusive.html)<'_, T, F>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#2305-2307)

#### pub fn [split_inclusive](https://docs.rs#method.split_inclusive)<F>(&self, pred: F) -> [SplitInclusive](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/iter/struct.SplitInclusive.html)<'_, T, F>

Returns an iterator over subslices separated by elements that match
`pred`. The matched element is contained in the end of the previous
subslice as a terminator.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-28)Examples

```
let slice = [10, 40, 33, 20];
let mut iter = slice.split_inclusive(|num| num % 3 == 0);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &[10, 40, 33]);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &[20]);
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
If the last element of the slice is matched, that element will be considered the terminator of the preceding slice. That slice will be the last item returned by the iterator.

```
let slice = [3, 10, 40, 33];
let mut iter = slice.split_inclusive(|num| num % 3 == 0);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &[3]);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &[10, 40, 33]);
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
Returns an iterator over subslices separated by elements that match
`pred`, starting at the end of the slice and working backwards.
The matched element is not contained in the subslices.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-29)Examples

```
let slice = [11, 22, 33, 0, 44, 55];
let mut iter = slice.rsplit(|num| *num == 0);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &[44, 55]);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &[11, 22, 33]);
assert_eq!(iter.next(), None);
```
As with `split()`, if the first or last element is matched, an empty
slice will be the first (or last) item returned by the iterator.

```
let v = &[0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8];
let mut it = v.rsplit(|n| *n % 2 == 0);
assert_eq!(it.next().unwrap(), &[]);
assert_eq!(it.next().unwrap(), &[3, 5]);
assert_eq!(it.next().unwrap(), &[1, 1]);
assert_eq!(it.next().unwrap(), &[]);
assert_eq!(it.next(), None);
```
Returns an iterator over subslices separated by elements that match
`pred`, limited to returning at most `n` items. The matched element is
not contained in the subslices.

The last element returned, if any, will contain the remainder of the slice.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-30)Examples

Print the slice split once by numbers divisible by 3 (i.e., `[10, 40]`,
`[20, 60, 50]`):

```
let v = [10, 40, 30, 20, 60, 50];
for group in v.splitn(2, |num| *num % 3 == 0) {
    println!("{group:?}");
}
```
Returns an iterator over subslices separated by elements that match
`pred` limited to returning at most `n` items. This starts at the end of
the slice and works backwards. The matched element is not contained in
the subslices.

The last element returned, if any, will contain the remainder of the slice.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-31)Examples

Print the slice split once, starting from the end, by numbers divisible
by 3 (i.e., `[50]`, `[10, 40, 30, 20]`):

```
let v = [10, 40, 30, 20, 60, 50];
for group in v.rsplitn(2, |num| *num % 3 == 0) {
    println!("{group:?}");
}
```
[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#2528-2530)#### pub fn [split_once](https://docs.rs#method.split_once)<F>(&self, pred: F) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<(&[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html), &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html))>

`slice_split_once`)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#2528-2530)

#### pub fn [split_once](https://docs.rs#method.split_once)<F>(&self, pred: F) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<(&[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html), &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html))>

`slice_split_once`)Splits the slice on the first element that matches the specified predicate.

If any matching elements are present in the slice, returns the prefix
before the match and suffix after. The matching element itself is not
included. If no elements match, returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-32)Examples

```
#![feature(slice_split_once)]
let s = [1, 2, 3, 2, 4];
assert_eq!(s.split_once(|&x| x == 2), Some((
    &[1][..],
    &[3, 2, 4][..]
)));
assert_eq!(s.split_once(|&x| x == 0), None);
```

`slice_split_once`)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#2557-2559)

#### pub fn [rsplit_once](https://docs.rs#method.rsplit_once)<F>(&self, pred: F) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<(&[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html), &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html))>

`slice_split_once`)Splits the slice on the last element that matches the specified predicate.

If any matching elements are present in the slice, returns the prefix
before the match and suffix after. The matching element itself is not
included. If no elements match, returns `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-33)Examples

```
#![feature(slice_split_once)]
let s = [1, 2, 3, 2, 4];

    &[1, 2, 3][..],
    &[4][..]
)));
assert_eq!(s.rsplit_once(|&x| x == 0), None);
```
Returns `true` if the slice contains an element with the given value.

This operation is *O*(*n*).

Note that if you have a sorted slice, [ binary_search](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.binary_search) may be faster.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-34)Examples

```
let v = [10, 40, 30];
assert!(v.contains(&30));
assert!(!v.contains(&50));
```
If you do not have a `&T`, but some other value that you can compare
with one (for example, `String` implements `PartialEq<str>`), you can
use `iter().any`:

```
let v = [String::from("hello"), String::from("world")]; // slice of `String`
assert!(v.iter().any(|e| e == "hello")); // search with `&str`
assert!(!v.iter().any(|e| e == "hi"));
```
1.0.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/slice/mod.rs.html#2624-2626)#### pub fn [starts_with](https://docs.rs#method.starts_with)(&self, needle: &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)
